review: As a woman in my 60ies it was fun to become a pirate, I felt like a less annoying Keira Knightley sailing about with Johnny Depp. This game was harder than the first but once again I did great and kicked its butt. I can beat everyone, I've still got it.

The game is a masterpiece, just like the first one. After finishing PoE 1, I immediately started with the second one and I was treated to another marvel of a game. Here are some of my thoughts:

The Good:
-Very good main story but the side content is what made this game great
-Interesting and deep characters, both new ones and some returning from the first game, including companions
-The story picks up after the events of the first game and is a direct continuation of the first game (just like with Baldur’s Gate 1 and 2)
-If you still have the savegame-files from the first game, your decisions and consequences from the first game will carry over
-There is so much lore, if you are into reading and listening to stories
-A lot of voice-acting
-A lot of pets you can collect and the equipped one has a small benefit to your party
-Interesting races and sub-races, each with its own boons and downsides
-Interesting classes and sub-classes, including the possibility of multi-classes
-You can retrain your characters
-You can make a new character to join your party at any time at tavern
-Item and weapon diversity (including pistols)
-You have the option to play the game as either turn-based (like divinity original sin) or real time (with game pause, just like Baldur’s Gate)
-You can sail the seas as a pirate and attack any ship you meet without consequence. The ships on the map will respawn endlessly so you will never run out, which makes them a real great source of income.
-Besides the ship you are given at the beginning, there are a few others you can buy. Each has its own benefits
-Ship, crew and sailing require some management, but if you like this sort of stuff you can get real invested in it 
-Exploring the map by ship, if you are into that kind of stuff
-When engaging other ships, you have a choice between boarding or naval combat
-Endurance is no longer a thing so you only need to manage your Health during fights. You will like this if you were not a big fan of the Endurance vs Health system from the first game
-The resting system has improved. Besides taverns, now you can rest anywhere you want as long as you have food
-No inventory management is necessary. Your inventory is infinite so just pick everything up because sooner or later you might need things like explosives, potions, tools etc.
-Choice matters, and boy are there a lot of different paths you can choose from
-Romance options
-Bounties are fun and offer good experience and money
-DLCs are a bit shorter than the one from the first game, but they are just as good (will not describe them to avoid spoilers)

The Bad:
-Loading screens are too long and too many
-Just like in the first game, I reached max level at about 2/3 of the game(max level 20) so any experience gathered beyond that was pointless. By the end of the game could have easily reached level 30 if that was a thing
-Naval combat is scripted, so it might not be as spectacular as you might imagine
-Exploring islands on foot isn’t so much fun
-The idea of factions might not be to everyone’s liking
-After playing for a few hours, the game performance seems to decrease and my pc struggled with running it. Maybe the game has an optimization problem but it’s possibly that this one is on me and the game is fine. This might not be the case for other users.

Advice:
-In the beginning of the game, try to reach Neketaka asap and do as many quests there as you can before heading out on your ship exploring the seas
-Pick everything up. Your inventory space is infinite and you will end up needing diverse items like explosives, traps, tools etc.
-Always have tools with you: hammer and chisel, prybar, lockpicks, grappling hook. You will really need them from time to time
-Plundering other ships is a great source of experience, resources and money but be careful not to burn yourself out if you do it for too long
-If you get stuck on a quest, just do some online research
-Invest money in your ship and crew as soon as you can
-Always have a tank and healer in the party
-Make sure to diversify the skills of your party. It’s always good to have someone with Mechanics, Religion, Athletics or Diplomacy most of all
-Enchant your items
-When you get the white/grey colored legendary items, make sure to bind them to the character you equip them on and do the mini-quests inscribed on them to unlock new powers and features
-Use summons, as they are great for distracting enemies. They can take a lot of hits and also dish it out

My game experience:
I played on the classic (normal) difficulty, just like I do with every new game I start, and found the game not very hard but fun. I played the game in real time, because turn-based takes too long. As soon as I got my first ship working, I sailed to Neketaka, found the last companions I knew I wanted on my permanent team (Maia and Pallegina) and just quested away in the city until I had enough money and levels under my belt to start exploring the seas and attack other ships. I never did the scripted naval combat because I was having too much fun boarding the ships and watch my characters fight. My party consisted of my Watcher (Moon Godlike, Chanter, specced in summoning), Eder (because he’s a beast of a tank and has some fun interactions with others), Xoti (gotta have a healer, she’s also fun to have around), Maia Rua (very good ranged DPS and she comes with a pet cause she’s a ranger) and Pallegina, who is an excellent off-tank and support character. Once I took to the seas, I made my fortune by plundering ships, equipped my ship and characters with the best money could buy and then just catered to the different existing factions in the Deadfire, while not loosing sight of my main mission.

I had a great time playing Pillars of Eternity 1 and 2. I consider they offer some great replay value and are great fun if you are into this style of RPG games. If you are a fan of games like the Baldur’s Gate, Icewind Dale, Diablo, Dragon Age, Neverwinter Nights and Divinity Original Sin series, you must try PoE 1 and 2.
I really hope they make Pillars of Eternity 3.

This is an absolutely amazing game, one of the very best of it's kind. As it happens, I never played the first POE but I have enjoyed this so much. This is right up there with the best in it's genre, like DOS/DOS2. I came straight from Divinity Original Sin 2 to this. As a result, I thought I would prefer the newly released turn based mode, but it felt far too slow for me. Before going any farther, I immediately created a new game in the original RTWP mode, and haven't looked back.

I have sunk soooo many more hours than I would've thought possible into this game, 300+, and that's just a single playthrough. There are tons of other companions I didn't touch, DLCs I haven't gotten to yet, and I haven't quite finished the main story either. There is a huge amount of replayability here. With the amount of content, hours played, and enjoyment I got from this game, I feel like this should've cost me several hundred dollars.

If you like these types of games, you will really enjoy POE2, and it is absolutely worth full price.

Pros: 
     1.) In-text definition
     2.) Graphics
     3.) Gameplay

In-text definitions: 
      This was one of the neatest integrations that they could've made.  I like the fact that 
       Obsidian took the time to add defintions for a lot of the different names, etc. that new 
       people would have to look up.  This game is very lore heavy, as it should be, so there are 
       a lot of areas, etc. that new players would have to look up themselves.  I don't find 
       any issue with it looking up stuff on my other computer while being in-game, but some 
       might so I wanted to mention that.  The in-text definitions are awesome.   
 
Graphics/Gameplay:
       The game looks great and plays well.  I'm playing on max settings and have only had a 
        few drops in framerate coming out of a cutscene or loading screen.  Outside of that, the 
        game runs smooth.

Skill tree: 
        The skill tree for this game is something that will take getting used to for the newbies like 
        myself.  There are a lot of damage over time, CC and damage reduction nodes to be 
        explore, making many different options for creating a well synchronized party. 

Cons:
     1.) Misspellings
     2.) Sound distortion  
     3.) Loading screens

Cons Explored:
     Misspellings:
         I can't say that misspellings broke the immersion for me, but for those that are very 
         particular about that sort of thing, then you might get triggered a little.  However, I ask 
         that you look past the latter because the story is extremely good...so far.
    
Sound distortion:
         I am unsure if anyone else experienced distortion in the sound quality within segments 
         of the narrative, but I did find a few.  Also, a couple instances where the volume was low 
         for the first half of a sentence then got loud for the 
         second half.  Personally, that wasn't a big deal for me, but I know how particular some 
         people are, so I just want to throw that out there.
 Loading screens:
          I won't lie, there are a lot of loading screens in this game and I have only put in 11 hours 
          so far.  The issue with this is that it takes away from up-time in-game, with some being

CONCLUSION:
          Awesome and deep (story-wise) game so far.  I'm not one for giving out artificial scores,

          a very extensive and detailed skill tree and meaningful choices then you have found the

SUMMARY: If you've played any games in the Baldur's Gate series and liked them, then you'll most likely enjoy this game. Pillars of Eternity 2 definitely has some different mechanics compared to the BG games, and not all of them are for the better, to be honest...but many are. It can take some getting used to, but if you're patient (and most RPG-ers are), you'll be rewarded with a sweet adventure, solid characters (mostly), great music, and an overall fun time that you can easily sink dozens of enjoyable hours into.

The main complaint I have about this game is that many things that are either critical to truly understanding the game's mechanics, or critical to being able to progress through a couple points, are quite poorly explained. An example of the former: damage type (and hence weapon type) can be EXTREMELY critical to whether your characters are effective in combat, or near useless in a few key fights.
An example of the latter: in later versions of this game, there is a certain ship upgrade that is ONLY available at two particular places. And for story reasons, it's quite likely you'll end up eliminating one of those two sources. That will leave you with literally ONE shop in the game left to buy the critical upgrade. But unless you figure out that you can actually access a shop menu from the game's island map screen - which is never explained to you in game (so far as I know) and you'd never think to do, because what imaginary merchant are you buying from on the map screen? - then you'll NEVER accrue the needed upgrade.
Were it not for the game's message boards, I never would have discovered this.

A few differences in game mechanics compared to the Baldur's Gate games (hardly an exhaustive list):
1.) Equipment choices are generally less restrictive in PoE2. You can equip even a mage with the heaviest armor, for example, although it's usually a bad idea to do so, because heavy armor has the highest recovery time. But still, you have the option to do so if you'd like. In the Baldur games, mages just flat out couldn't use heavy armor (barring certain fighter-mage combinations).
2.) In the BG games, you had to rest for 8 hours in order to recover expended spells. In PoE2, spells are automatically replenished once you "complete" a battle. This is a welcome difference that frankly makes spell casters considerably more useful than they were in the BG games. Because your mages will actually be able to cast a significant number of spells, rather than in BG where you were forced to either rest constantly, or only use spells for the more critical moments of your battles.
3.) Enemy encounters are a bit fewer than in BG, but each encounter will (on average) also be more challenging.
4.) No more carry weight limits, or limits on how many items you can carry at once.
5.) It's much harder to cheese your way through fights. In Baldur's Gate, you could often win tough fights by luring one particular enemy away from its pack, isolate it, and then have everyone attack it; rinse and repeat for the rest of the enemies. While this is still (to a degree) possible in PoE2, it's much harder to pull off. So combat in PoE2 tends to be more of a true test of skill, and less about micromanagement and cheesery.

In closing, Pillars of Eternity 2 is DEFINITELY a good game you should play if you like isometric RPGs, Baldur's Gate, or epic quests that can require some patience. PoE2 has its flaws, it definitely doesn't explain (or at least emphasize) things as well as it should sometimes, and due to the freedom of movement you're given early on in the game, you can REALLY struggle through certain portions of the game if you attempt certain side quests in the wrong order (as I apparently did). But it's a fun game worth playing and re-playing. TRY IT!

If you liked Pillars of Eternity you oughta like Deadfire, but even if you didn't like Pillars of Eternity there's a chance you will like the sequel.


Deadfire retains some qualities of Pillars of Eternity. The writing is still very strong with immersive world-building and engaging storytelling. Role-playing options are still plentiful, with an even bigger emphasis on dialogue and character choices. (The "main" questline is really only a few quests, with much of your time dedicated to navigating the sociopolitical conflicts of warring factions and ultimately deciding who will control the archipelago after the world's been saved.) Unfortunately, your companions are still a little bland. It's a particular shame because with the inclusion of "sidekicks" you have so many more friends joining you on your journey. I don't know if it's the writing or the performances that cause me to be unimpressed, but, with the exception of Eder and Aloth (and maybe Xoti), the companions just don't engage me much.

But Deadfire does change things up a bit from Pillars of Eternity, and in my opinion they're all positive changes:

Combat is still micromanage-y, but with improved A.I. options. There are also incremental options to adjust the speed of combat to your liking. [I cannot speak on the Turn-Based combat mode, as I did not use it, but even having the option is nice.]

Gameplay in general just feels smoother and more lively. (Though there is some unintuitive interface design—e.g., switching out companions while in a settlement is mind-boggling awkward and requires way too many clicks.)

Important story "cutscenes" feature gorgeous hand-drawn—well, digital, but you know what I mean—art that really bring the gods and their realms to life with a lot of color.

The biggest thing, however, is the setting, which is much more exciting and brings many welcome changes. No more drab meadows and generic castles—nay, this time we're on the open seas, full of privateers, pirates, oceanic phenomena, and uncharted islands to discover. The new setting means Deadfire is a much more visually stimulating game. The world is full of blue waters, lush jungles, arid deserts, mucky swamps, volcanic isles, vibrant corals, and beautiful architecture inspired by Pacific-islander cultures. This setting is populated by a wider variety of peoples, and you'll be able to immerse yourself in their many cultures and histories. (Although it does feel a bit repetitive that two societies sound vaguely Italian/vaguely French.) Another setting-related change is the replacement of your stronghold with a ship, which is fully manageable, requiring upgrades, crew, and supplies, all of which can be acquired through the many ports. Having a ship also means there's naval combat, which is... merely serviceable. The actual ship-on-ship combat is disappointingly shallow, but that's why you always skip to boarding: it never stops being satisfying to board an enemy ship, slay the crew, and loot their treasures. It's this swashbuckling atmosphere the Deadfire Archipelago promises that initially drew me to the game, and I'm happy to say it mostly didn't disappoint.


So in summary, if you enjoyed Pillars of Eternity and want more, or are simply looking for an engaging story that ponders philosophical and theological questions and asks you to make difficult decisions, then hurry up and play Deadfire. If you weren't won over by Pillars of Eternity, but your issues were mostly with the bland presentation, then I'd recommend giving it a try. If you didn't like Pillars of Eternity at all, well, feel free to pass.


[P.S. wrt to DLC: The Beast of Winter, good; Slayer Seeker Survivor, meh; Forgotten Sanctum, good.]

Spoiler free review. 

Straight away I want to mention a few things:

1. The main story is VERY short.
2. MANY side quests - if not all - relate back to the main quest.
3. The above two points can be ignored if you choose to simply do the main quest, in otherwords, the game is as long as you want it to be.

DIFFICULTY

Strange thing about Pillars of Eternity II: Deadfire (Deadfire) is that I found it extremely easy.  There are 5 difficulty settings to choose from. I suggest starting your game on the hardest difficulty because once you get going in the game, not much is going to be able to stop you, especially, when you get comfortable with the AI editor (more on that later).

Separate from the main difficulty settings, throughout your campaign you'll unlock achievements which grant you "blessings". These blessings can be spent on a variety of additional options/changes to change the game for a second playthrough, some could be seen as minor, others huge.

Again, separate from the main difficulty settings, you also have "Magran's Fires". Magran's Fires is a selection of options you are able to turn on or off that challenge the player in a major way eg by turning on "Galawain's Challenge", "beasts gain powerful effects".

CHARACTER CREATION

A different thing that Deadfire does is that multiclassing a character has to selected at character creation. There is no way to add a second class once your character has been created. Personally, this didn't faze me at all but I can imagine some people would like to know this before starting.

Everything is laid out before you during character creation and with each level up you gain which is fantastic. There's no guessing what spells a class could learn, or what fighting stances your tank will have to pick from > it's all there for you to see from the start so you can literally plan a character out from the word "go" (including your companions).

THE SET UP

Deadfire allows players to continue their game from a Pillars of Eternity save. This can have massive effects in Deadfire. Characters might be dead or relocated to a completely different area with differing opinions about certain things in the Deadfire world.

If like me, you've never played Pillars of Eternity, you get to select what your character was like in Pillars of Eternity via answering questions posed to you.

Lore, lore and more lore... plus extra lore. There's sooooooo much lore in Deadfire that if handled in a particular manner (or simply poorly) this game would/could drown it's players into submission. Thankfully this is never the case. Deadfire handles lore in all the ways you'd expect, via books, branching conversations, environmental story telling, pages of the stuff in menus for you to read etc. The lore is - like the games duration - is as deep as you want to make it.

Much of - if not everything - about Deadfire is what you make of it. To mention only a small handful of things you can choose to do:

* Hire a crew
* Buy ships
* Sail the seas
* Discover islands > and name them
* Take note that there's multiple types of currency (the game auto sorts it for you)
* Buy your favorite snacks
* Have an all male crew onboard? Listen to an all male crew sea shanty > change it to an all female crew and listen to an all female crew sea shanty. How about changing your crew to a personality trait and listening that style of shanty etc.

COMBAT

There two types of in-game combat, regular combat and ship vs ship combat.

Ship combat is a script based combat system where you will pick instructions on what you want your crew to do eg fire port cannons, turn left and change crew positions onboard etc. Many people didn't like this system and I can see why. It takes a long time in comparison to simply ramming your enemies ship and attacking them in regular combat.

I wouldn't say I disliked the ship combat, I just found it tiresome after giving it more than its fair share of a turn.

Regular combat gives you two options, turn based and real time with pause. I played the game using the real time with pause. Real time with pause is where the AI editor really shines. The AI editor allows you to select what your individual team mates will do as an individual in any and all separate situations. I loved it.... kinda over powered but it works amazingly > USE IT.

YOUR TEAM

You have companions and sidekicks. Companions are a mix of new faces and companions from the first game whereas sidekicks are all new faces. Most - if not all - companions and sidekicks are directly associated with an in-game faction which can and will have interesting twists and turns.

Some of the companions and sidekicks have unique traits such as being able to turn into a man-shark-thing which only they can do. Every member of your team feels unique and alive.

PLOT

I'm not going to spoil anything in-game. What I will say is that the story is built upon 4 main factions which pull and tear at eachother, constantly in a flux of weariness. Each faction has their clear strengths and weaknesses. Within these factions, there's sub factions. There's political intrigue, sabotage, assassinations, grey moral decisions at EVERY turn (to such an extent, I have no idea if I got what could be considered a good or bad ending... or even if such a thing can exist in the Deadfire universe).

In short the plot is really good. There's plenty of food for thought and self reflection within.

DLC

I love them all. There're loads, some of which is simply small DLC such as more haircuts but the story DLC adds even more lore to the world. They all start in the end game phase so if you buy the DLC, don't feel worried you've missed something to do with the DLC when you hit level 16 with your character (level 20 is max and I started the DLC at level 18 on average across all my characters).

BAD STUFF

The icons in the inventory are way too small. I found it fiddly at best when trying to locate something. I did get used to it but still, it's a bit "meh" as far as inventory screens goes.

The AI editor is too good. Don't get me wrong, I loved it! however, I can see at the same time that it's way too good. A lot of fights literally required no interaction at all from myself other-than a single click to tell my squad to engage an enemy (bosses included). Everything can be automated which could for some - not me - take away something from the game.

FINAL THOUGHTS

I bought this on sale and had no idea what I was getting myself into. I loved it. Due to the lore, this is now one of my favorite RPG games. Fact is, I liked it so much that I bought the first game with all it's DLC and plan to start that next and continue my save file into the Deadfire.

Link to my review of the first game, Pillars of Eternity, at the bottom.

Before my purchase, I was curious and hopeful that this was going to be better than Pathfinder, a game that I liked up until the last couple of hours. From my perspective, Deadfire is way better by leaps and bounds.

Obsidian Entertainment’s follow-up to the massively successful [b]Pillars of Eternity[/b] that was released last 2015. The Watcher, armed with a ship and in the company of a motley crew of characters, must fight, convince, or connive his way to reach Eothas. But as you, the player does so, getting caught into the web of politics, betrayals, and 'go to X and do Y' quests. The Deadfire Archipelago is filled with the unknown and yet unexplored lands. Four factions vie for control of the isles with each one having their own agendas and plans.

[b][i]Pillars of Eternity II: Deadfire[/i][/b] is and has always been conceived as a modern take on the 2D text-based RPGs of the 1990s. It is played with a top-down view and static camera, partnered with long lines of texts that can either enrich your vocabulary or irreparably cross your eyes altogether.

The game mainly uses the combat mechanics found in the first [b]Pillars of Eternity[/b]. Each character has a recovery period which is determined by their previous action, their equipment, and their stats. Once the bar depletes the character can execute a move. You can also just leave things to the AI but this kind of approach isn’t recommended especially on higher levels of difficulty. Manually placing your units and giving them their commands during intense parts of combat is key in winning.

One huge departure from the first game is the introduction of ships as home bases. Here, the player can manage party composition, resources, and character interaction. Wandering across the seas of Deadfire requires both manpower and resources.

[b][i]Pillars of Eternity II: Deadfire[/i][/b] may not be for everyone. First obvious reason would be its slow-burn pacing. With its world, taking everything into account and absorbing it takes time.

[b][i]Pillars of Eternity II: Deadfire[/i][/b] is a beautiful and thoroughly enjoyable RPG, one which I'd happily recommend. If you loved the first [b]Pillars of Eternity[/b], you’ll definitely love this one.

- Balanced real-time combat
- Fascinating depth and detail to the world

- Ship-to-ship combat is a letdown

Best CRPG I've ever played. One of the best games I've ever played, in general. 

For some context: I grew up playing Neverwinter Nights and Dragon Age Origins. I got back into CRPG's through Divinity Original Sin 2, however I didn't love how sandbox-y/sometimes silly that game felt. There was a focus on puzzles and metagaming, rather than immersion and role playing. I also LOVE real-time-with-pause. I played Baldur's Gate 1 + 2, which were fun but dated, and honestly some of the gameplay in Baldur's Gate 2 was so convoluted and obscure that it felt like the only way to enjoy the game was on a second playthrough once you know how to prepare for each zone. Pathfinder was buggy and had timers and kingdom management which turned me off. 

Which brings me to Pillars 1 + 2. I played Pillars 1 and fell in love with the game. The atmosphere was perfect, the systems were fresh and felt designed around being a fun videogame rather than trying to take an existing system and make a videogame around it. However, I wanted more. I wanted more depth, more story, more exploration, more variety. Pillars 2 scratched that itch. 

It's hard for me to think of this game without getting excited about all of the different ways you can create a character. It feels like there are infinite options, each one well thought out and on a standard difficulty, it feels almost difficult to go wrong! That's a huge achievement for this genre. The gameplay is a blast. Changing abilities to per-encounter from per-rest was a huge improvement alone, and should be the standard for CRPG's. 

The story is wonderful. I read a lot of comments from Gamers™ who complain about moral ambiguity, or that the characters they want to support morally are not likeable enough. For me and for that reason, I found this to be one of the most honest depictions of colonialism/imperialism in gaming. It does not fall into a noble savage trope. It often goes out of its way to create friendly and likeable characters who support the colonial powers. It makes you think about your choices in the context of what is moral and ethical for the game world, not just for your favorite characters. I think it's bravely written and very interesting, far more interesting than a stock fantasy story. And yet, it doesn't subdue its fantastical elements which stays front and center in both gameplay and story. 

10/10

Pillars of Eternity 2 doesn't have the great companions, the charismatic antagonist or the packed content of Baldur's Gate II. It doesn't have the riveting storyline of Planescape Torment. In terms of party building, Pathfinder: Kingmaker has it beat in depth. And Divinity: Original Sin II, though being strictly turn-based, has more care put into its encounters than PoE2. 

Deadfire is not a perfect game. The main story is quite short. If you don't stick around for some sidequests, I reckon you could beat the game in 15 hours or so. The majority of the sidequests take place in the capital city of Neketaka, which serves as a hub, much like Athkatla in BG2, albeit Neketaka doesn't have nearly as many secrets as BG2's city. The ship battles are very lackluster, to say the least: I strongly recommend simply boarding enemy ships if you're faced with the dilemma.

It's been years since its initial release, and there are still bugs here and there, though not enough to ruin a playthrough. The most memorable I suffered through was aggroing a number of important quest NPCs by entering an area from the "wrong" way, which would've locked me out of an entire faction's questline had it not fixed itself magically after... something happened? Not quite sure.

What PoE2 DOES have going for it, though, is a very solid experience that stays good throughout; take the games I mentioned earlier. Planescape's Crust area, near the end of the game, is considered by many to be the worse part of the game. Kingmaker's entire second half is filled with annoying encounters and ridiculous party member deaths if you don't fill arbitrary conditions (and in some cases, straight up deaths). D:OS2's Act 4 is a complete letdown after the grandiose Act 1 and content-packed Act 2 from that game. But Deadfire, at least in my opinion, manages to stick the landing, especially if one plays the DLCs, two of which I heartily recommend (Beast of Winter and Forgotten Sanctum both have interesting storylines and challenging boss fights).

My favorite aspect of the combat is the abiltiy to setup your party's AI, choose what skills to use and what skills to forbid, etc. This meant I could trust my spellcasters and my healers to act appropriately, and let me micromanage my frontliners (Monk and Fighter) without worries. The result was that I could simply let the AI handle the random grunts and mobs, and actually put my thinking cap on for the more challenging encounters out there (side note, PoE2 is on the easy side of the CRPG genre: if you're thinking of playing it on Normal, crank it up to Hard, if you're trying to check it out on Easy, play it on Normal, etc.).

As far as companions go, they're okay. The characters from the first game get some more time in the spotlight, but their personal quest (singular) is short and doesn't really go in-depth. Compared to PoE1's companion questlines, the ones in PoE2 are a bit lacking, which is a shame. But hey, on the gameplay side, everytime you recruit a sidekick (companions... but without the personal quests, noice), you get to choose between two single classes and a multiclass option! Very cool.

The setting of the Deadfire archipelago, with four factions vying for control, left me hooked, much like New Vegas did. You have the Huana (natives of the Deadfire), the Principi (pirates), the Vailian Trading Company (think something like the Italian Republics) and the Royal Deadfire Company (think Imperial Japan), and each of them have their flaws and their own questlines, which I found to be the most interesting aspect of the game. 

Other points: the first game could sometimes be very wordy and made it hard to keep track of all the names and the comings and goings, but PoE2's way more concise and respectful of your time. The existence of a fast forward button is a godsend: turn it on and leave it on. The lack of a nice big dungeon to explore in the base game is a shame, since those tend to be my favorite parts of CRPGs (think chapter 3 of Kingmaker, or pretty much every area in the Baldur's games), but the DLCs thankfully had my back. UNFORTUNATELY the load times are absolutely unbearable, so unless you have an SSD, steel yourself.

With how often this game goes on sale with the DLCs bundled, it's pretty easy to get it for a steal of a price. Shoutouts to my buddy Enh for pushing me into playing the PoE games, wouldn't have seen the light otherwise.

For me Baldur´s Gate 2 is the best story driven, party management, isometric RPG that I have ever played (Fallout 1 and 2, and Arcanum being other two worth mentioning). 

I loved Divinity Original Sin I and II and Baldur´s Gate 3. Larian did an amazing job. But there was just something missing - every step of the way I felt I could conquer everything with ease as an experienced RPG player. No anxiety, no excitement, no fear of the unknown. 

But not in this game. That fear of the unknown, of being underpowered, of: "oh no, there is another set of stairs going down, and my characters are broken, beat, and scarred already...should I turn back?". That is what for me makes an RPG of this type truly great. The feeling of being lost, overpowered, looking for strategic solutions, some crazy tactic to win, and all that on the seventh underground floor of some random dungeon, on some random island, where initially you just went to collect some free water and food. It makes it so much more rewarding and enjoyable once you win, and once you become a bully. 

This game combines the best from BG 2 and Arcanum. It reminds me of both. It is not as flashy as Larian games, but boy in my opinion it is much more fun and exciting to play. The lore, the atmosphere, the setting, just perfect. 

For the first time in 15-20 years I have that feeling of excitement and anxiety at the same time when playing an RPG of this time (I exclude Dark Souls, Morrowind and Gothic from this talk, because they are not RPGs of the same type). 

10/10.

Pillars of Eternity II: Deadfire is a very hard game to give my opinion on. I loved Pillars I more than words can describe, it was a truly excellent game. And, in some ways, Pillars II is an improvement over the first. The combat has been nicely streamlined, the UI has seen nice improvements, and the sheer volume of voice acting is marvelous. Unfortunately, this is where my praise ends. 

Pillars II sacrificed a lot in chasing the ambition of a more open-world experience and I think this was greatly to it's detriment. The series shines most in intricately designed, linear encounters that inspire wonder and interest from the player. Something that Deadfire severely lacks. So many areas feel poorly considered and rushed. Instead of having 8 excellent dungeons the game has 16 mediocre ones. In their attempts to make the world feel more full Obsidian instead made it feel as wide as an ocean and as deep as a pond. Exploring the Deadfire becomes, mostly, a completionist chore. The combat encounters are largely randomly generated and take place in huge, open battlefields that are reused multiple times and give no tactical depth. The wonder of the setting is quickly lost as this becomes more and more apparent and the player begins to notice how thinly worn Obsidian's efforts were. The setting is ambitious and fun, but fails to deliver because it falls outside of the scope that Pillars works best in.

The problems only cascade when you realize that exploring off the beaten path is actually a grave mistake. I managed to bug multiple important questlines by doing things out of order and in ways the developers didn't consider. I played an incredibly lawful character throughout Pillars I and continued this trend in Deadfire. Pirates attempting to ally and work with me? I deny them at every turn and tell them to fuck off. Turns out, killing them immediately like I would prefer leads to me missing out on important development and the ending that involves my character choosing to eliminate the pirates. Ok, so I'll wait. Good think I looked it up. They ask me to go help some slavers. I'm morally against slavery, obviously, so I infiltrate their walls and slaughter them. Turns out, this also broke a bunch of quests from people that, 20 hours later, decided they should give me a quest to eliminate the slavers. A lot of quests have problems like this. The player is railroaded as this rough n tough pirate that doesn't and shouldn't care about the morals of what they're doing. They're playing in a funny, happy-go-lucky swashbuckling setting! But I didn't treat the game like that and ended up largely disappointed by the choices I was forced to make and the people the game expected and desperately attempted to make me ally with. I think this is also a case of development resources being spread too thin. Many situations felt ill-considered and underdeveloped with a large lack of satisfying or varied choices offered to the player. So many quests ended disappointingly and had very little lasting consequence. The main story, on the other hand, was incredibly enjoyable and very satisfying, especially for players importing from Pillars I. I only wish we could have seen more quests like it in the game.

I think that Deadfire suffers deeply from it's failed attempts to make the overly large, empty world feel more full and alive than it is. I wholly believe that Obsidian could catch lightning in a bottle once more if they pulled back the scale of the sequel and made it more linear, if we ever get a 3rd main Pillars game. The world Obsidian has crafted in Eora is incredibly compelling and enjoyable to explore, I simply believe that Deadfire fails to do it justice by stretching itself too thin. I would still recommend this game, despite it's flaws. It's more of the same great formula I loved in Pillars I, but it's by no means the 10/10 experience the first game offered. If you liked that game, you'll likely enjoy this one too. Please buy it so Obsidian can take another crack at a, hopefully, more focused aspect of Eora's world!

Put simply, PoE:Deadfire is a vastly improved sequel to the original Pillars of Eternity, featuring massively expanded class options, hefty replay value, and an optional turn-based combat system alongside its active one. Despite its good points, however, the game is noticeably less polished than its predecessor (downright broken in some areas) removes the castle management, and reduces the party size by one. It also sold so poorly that it nearly killed Obsidian and gave poor J.E. Sawyer an existential crisis.

But you don't care about that, do you?

You want to know if this fantasy RPG lets you run roughshod over the seas as a pirate, going on pirate adventures with pirate ship battles in search of pirate treasure. You want know if you can date hot merpeople, sentient swords, and nerdy elf vampires. You want to know if you can cave in an ogre's face with a psychically-augmented blunderbuss. You want to know if you can ambush a viking longship full of fire giants with your lovingly-customized galleon's arsenal of double-barrel cannons manned by a freakish assortment of collected NPCs taken from the warring factions you've played against one another, desperate to finish the fight before being overtaken by an apocalyptic storm keeping you away from a safe harbor where you can finally restock your food supply.

Hell yes, you can.

PoE2 is beautiful and underrated.
Terribly sad this game did not sell well and Tyranny was pretty overlooked. Larian and Owlcat are kind of the darlings of modern CRPGs right now, and they make great games no doubt, but I absolutely love Obsidian's style of CRPGs the most.
I can only hope we'll eventually get another one from them one day and PoE doesnt go the way of Fallout with Avowed taking Pillars into a first person, more "broader-reaching" rpg.
At least i'll always have PoE1 & 2 and Tyranny.

This game is incredible.

Pros:
- Great band of allies full of character to get to know.
- Gameplay of all kinds is incredibly polished and looks beautiful.
- Challenging but not eye-wateringly hard unless you want it to be.
- So much customisation for your character and party in general. You can play however you want.
- Brilliantly written, fully voiced story. Every single quest is written and worded so perfectly. Every interaction has nuance. 
- Your decisions actually MATTER.
- You don't need to have played the previous game (even though it's amazing) to jump right in and feel like you know the world.
- Did I mention that the voice acting is incredible??!?!

Cons:
- There is A LOT of jargon surrounding stats, combat and how your powers work. Specifically buffs and debuffs. Often you need to remind yourself by going through 2-3 menus to understand the impact of what your abilities might do.
- While you can 'respec' your character and your allies, many of your decisions (like your class and the classes of your allies) are permanent which is quite unforgiving.
- You can easily build your character very 'wrong' and suffer for it. So try and keep things simple for a first playthrough, because there is no turning back on your decisions.

TLDR: Buy this immediately. You won't see your friends and family for a month but it's worth it.

The first [i]Pillars of Eternity[/i] was an immense disappointment when I played it. The world building and overall story were interesting, yet the companions felt stilted and the narrative was continuously interrupted by kickstarter self inserts.

[i]Deadfire[/i] was thus an incredibly welcome surprise. The graphics are slightly overhauled with additional lighting & spell effects. This is noticeable in the very first area where a rainbow dances over a waterfall concealing a cavern. And was further validated by the delicate animations that bring each character to vivid life, whether it be flexing their water shaping skills, or scratching an itch in an... unmentionable area. The landscapes themselves evoke the Carribean, but with just enough innovation to still feel exotic, with Adra taking the place of coral to form reefs and shoals. Whilst exotic fruits & berries form the basis of various local cuisines. These little hints of the fantastical were present in the first game as well, but with the unusual setting they are even more apparent, & create an environment of discovery.

As tropical as the environments are, the game doesn't shy away from more graphical effects in combat as well. Spells are the most gorgeous to see, with bright neon colours dancing about the screen, whilst insidious cloud effects partially obscure the combatants. Even the fighters are well realised as they steady themselves before a dash attack, & launch themselves on their enemies. Critical hits have a kill cam feature where the game momentarily slows down time, before zooming in on the action further. The slow down however was rather frustrating as the combat wouldn't flow as smoothly after, and the loss of framerates at such times was immensely frustrating. 

At times when the action on screen was particularly frenetic, the UI certainly came to the fore. Most information is readily available and many of the pop up menus are contextual which is helpful. The game does highlight figures if you linger over them with the mouse and an information screen will also pop up giving general details such as resistances, current effects and a generalised statement of health.

Narratively the game attempts to wear many hats, it wants to be a postcolonial deconstruction of colonial economics, a rollicking marine adventure ala Robert Louis Stevenson, by way of Pirates of Penzance and a high fantasy RPG that delves into existentialism, the nature of the divine & at times even ecological terrorism. This kaleidoscope of influences collide into a mess of genres and tropes. A cohesive theme is lost in favour of attempting to straddle various genres and their requisite themes. Whilst this slew of influences lends the game it's diversity it also lessons the impact of any particular message the game might have.

The faction quests form the backbone to the God's secular question, of whether humanity itself is able to overcome its differences and act in unison to confront a global crisis. Eothas, in the aspect of Gaun, is simply the progenitor of this crisis and Woedica who is the most antagonistic and cynical about the nature of the kith, seems to be the most vindicated by the results of your actions at the end of the game. This is largely due to the fact that the game offers no true resolution to the factions. There is no armistice,  in fact it fails rather dismally, sometimes as a direct result of the players intervention. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1558504805
Gods, even the artificial gods of Eora, are clearly considered too much for the protagonist to handle. The game steers directly away from the power inherit within a protagonist to indicate, despite being a Watcher, that your abilities are mundane. This is done repeatedly; from tête-à-têtes with the 'Prevailing Powers That Be' to encounters with archmagi that reveal their superiority over the player character. Even the trials against gods take place as gauntlets to be overcome rather than climactic confrontations, which is all the more obvious in the DLC content. It's a realism that is surprising in such a game, and has been the source of many complaints, not least amongst them the inability to duel Eothas at the finale, which many felt robbed players of a final boss fight. 

The combat in Deadfire is immense fun. Breaking away from min-maxing elements, leaves room for experimentation with builds. Many things are still the same, a dexterous wizard is viable but might (physical strength) is a positive boon as well, because it directly translates to the damage output of spells. Likewise unconventional melee builds are possible as well, with fighters being able to include intelligence as a stat for Defensive fighters due to its bonuses to AoE. As much as the game does allow for such unconventionality though on harder difficulties it still favours more traditional builds.

With its nautical theme, it's unsurprising that the player is given a ship to steer about the sea. This is where factional alliances come into play. Depending on the colours you fly various ships will either ignore or attack you. Managing and outfitting your ship takes the place of usual keep management. In addition Deadfire also has you manage the crew for your ship. The larger the ships and the more crew you have, the more food and water they will require. The game also introduces morale, & preventing them from mutinying will require either victories at sea or more expensive rations, usually of an alcoholic nature. Yet it never really feels like it amounts to that much. The travel distances of the Deadfire Archipelago are so small as to make most of the rationing and strategical planning to be redundant, & by the late stages of the game, the ships are easy money sinks, since the loot has improved immeasurably making it easy to simply purchase up the rations required. 

The other important aspects to ships is of course exploration. The ships crew gains experience in an additional levelling system, as they encounter new regions, sights & survive encounters. The islands themselves are marked on the map for you and a subquest encourages you to "colonise" the lands. However main quest locations are marked & can be sailed to directly without exploration. Since the islands are discrete landmasses, they don't offer a feeling of scale when adventuring. They inevitably end up feeling more like once off encounters rather than integrated parts of a world. As such the wonder of discovery is inevitably lost to a list of check marks, something that the game tries to prevent with its detailed and inventive locales but never quite achieves.

Pillars of Eternity 2: Deadfire is overall an exceptional game, with sound combat, an incredible interfactional storyline, but is let down by some very serious issues, such as the lack of intriguing exploration, poorly developed ship combat & a story that places you in a passive role. It is however still one of the finest RPGs ever made, despite the passive role and weaknesses in the narrative but is held aloft by its own inventiveness & creativity

[b]Pillars of Eternity II: Deadfire[/b] is a decent RPG at best since it only falls short on one of the few aspects that makes the CRPG genre recognizable: Good Storywriting. I recommend this game to those who played and enjoyed the first title. If you haven’t played Pillars of Eternity 1 yet, I suggest picking that up first if story continuity matters to you. If not, then I would probably recommend this to any RTwP and TBM players.

[h1]REVIEW[/h1]

The game is quite a refreshing take on the RPG genre made by Obsidian Entertainment. It introduces stellar graphics while retaining the classic isometric atmosphere from old games like Baldur’s Gate along with gameplay mechanics that have been improved from Pillars of Eternity 1. Despite all of the things this game did right, there’s no mistaking that there are still issues with it whatsoever.

You’ll take the role of the Watcher where you set sail with the ship’s crew towards the Deadfire Archipelago to confront a destructive god that towers over any castles and fortresses. This chapter brings you to a long journey meeting new and familiar faces and making tough decisions - as it concludes to an ending that screams for another sequel. :^)

Unlike most modern RPGs that include character creation, PoE2’s story is a direct sequel to the first game with your PoE1 character. Some of the choices and traits you’ve made from PoE1 will be carried over to this game.

[b]STORY[/b]

[list][*]The lack of [b]PoE1 Context[/b] feels like it’s not meant to be played by those who have skipped or will skip the first game. It’s true that there are not that much significant effects from our previous decisions, but it’s the way how a lot of characters mention these past events from PoE1. It makes us think as if we've missed a lot due to its underwhelming "amnesia" dialogues.

[*]The Deadfire Archipelago, however, feels completely different from the first game’s setting, so expect a lot of new things that will expand on world building. Even though most of the [b]DLC Stories[/b] lack relevance to the main story, it expands on the lore of the game’s world:

[list][*][u]The Beast of Winter[/u] has an interesting plot, but it’s hardly relevant to the main story. It features witnessing the past events that occurred before PoE1. It’s a great questline for a more unique experience.

[*][u]Seeker, Slayer, Survivor[/u] is basically an arena DLC with several unique items. It sort of fills up the lack of civilization on this game’s world, but it only does so little to the main story. The repetitiveness is what made this feel like the weakest DLC regardless on how “unique” the fights are.

[*][u]The Forgotten Sanctum[/u] is something that any player should never miss when picking this game up. The start of it may feel out of place, but this DLC itself directly contributes to the main story which is quite rare in most RPGs these days. Expect a lot of reading... and book pile toppling.[/list]

[*]A part of what made the main story weak was due to it contradicting with [b]Player Exploration[/b]. As you play through the main quest, you may feel conflicted as to whether should you continue or do other side quests. Most of these side quests are barely progressive to the main goal. Beneficial, sure, but given the [u]early[/u] knowledge on the god's whereabouts, you could just keep on pursuing it. Thus, us players may end up not taking the main story's urgency seriously.[/list]

[b]GAMEPLAY[/b]

[list][*]The game’s [b]Combat Mechanics[/b] feel more fleshed out than its predecessor in terms of balance, but there are still abilities that favor more than the other as usual. That is only the case if we’re talking about RTwP. The Turn-based Mode mechanics, on the other hand, still have much more to improve when it comes to its design.

[*]The best part in my opinion is the [b]Class System[/b]. There's a huge pool of possibilities for you to choose with classes having subclasses given that multi-classing was introduced in this game. It’s possible to make a character that is almost unkillable in solo. We could even be a mage slayer while ironically using a mage’s grimoire.

[*]The [b]Companion System[/b] has its ups and downs. It contains a disposition system for each companion where they can change the way they think of you and your other comrades depending on your choice of actions/dialogues and your other companion’s responses.

On the other hand, most of the companion quests end abruptly. Perhaps it’s because of the lack of depth each delivers while they’re mostly too short to even be acknowledged by the players. Nonetheless, they have a lot to say throughout the game, dialogue-wise.

[*]One thing that somewhat spices up the story is the [b]Factions[/b] given how the main plot flows around these opposing groups. Each faction has its own ideology on taking over the region, but supporting either sides only gives conversation checks for very few dialogues. Only the epilogue would show an actual impact or outcome basing from your decisions, so the system has nothing much to offer other than faction-based shops and discounts.

[*]Lastly, the [b]Quests[/b] are quite expansive regardless of the huge bulk of bounty hunting this game offers. There are quests that go from two or more dialogue conversations in two areas up to raiding a base with two or more different outcomes.[/list]

[b]AESTHETICS[/b]

[list][*]During its release, this game had one of the best [b]Graphics[/b] in all Isometric CRPGs. The well-executed details on each asset combined with the others really makes one sweet eye candy. Though, there are still glitches and optimization issues to consider.

[*]I would stay in the main menu and leave it there for awhile just to listen to the music. The [b]Soundtracks[/b] may not be over-the-top, but it sets the right mood for this game.

[*]The fully [b]Voiced Dialogues[/b] are mostly well delivered by the voice actors, but there are still notable NPCs that just doesn’t seem to perform very well. There are also some missing audio to some dialogues. [/list]

[b]BUGS/GLITCHES[/b]

[list][*]It may be avoidable, but not following a certain flow or pattern could lead to a [b]Broken Quest[/b]. It happens when the quest progresses in a way that the game wasn't programmed to handle. It was reported on around 2 or 3 quests so far.

[*]There are a few [b]Visual Glitches[/b] that occur on the characters. Some will turn completely invisible and have their weapons seem like they’re floating around the character.

[*]I may have not experienced this given that I often only rely on quicksaves, but knowing that creating a named manual save could lead to a random [b]Manual Save Deletion[/b] is a let down for some unlucky players. It seems this only occurs when you make a named manual save that is similar to an existing manual save, but that's just me assuming things.[/list]

I can't imagine why this game didn't get the reception and earn the money that it deserved. All I can say, is that turn-based mode is certainly a better option when it comes to CRPGs. I finally picked this up long after TB mode was implemented and wow... it's an incredible game. The writing was akin to that of BG 1 & 2, the atmosphere, small cosmetic things (like a sheath for your weapon!), excellent rule system, etc make this game a gem and worth your attention. While the elusive word immersive is unique to each person this team really seemed to understand that it starts with the small things. The music, the lighting, the setting... I wish camping would be more like PF:KM but it works. 

As someone who picked up BG3 on day 1 of EA (of course), I hope that Larian looks at what was really good about previous CRPGs and takes ideas to incorporate. While DOS 2 is fantastic in every way.. there's a certain level of connectivity that occurs with the small things in a game. Getting lost in the map, unforgiving challenges that you accidentally stumbled into, characters that radiate personality and a story that begs you to read it and not just hit okay. Oftentimes you don't need gorgeously rendered completely 3d graphics to capture the mood. 

If you're craving a CRPG fix and were a fan of the BG's and DOS, and haven't played POE2 like me- do it. Great game by an excellent company. I only hope they learned from the low-ish sales and not given up.

It is difficult to describe this game without using POE1 as a point of reference. Moreover, I sort of assume that you know what an "isometric RPG" is. So you understand the base concepts of such a fixed angle view game. Contrary to POE1, which was real time combat only, you now have the option of turn-based combat which doesn't change the overall combat dynamic all that much, it just makes for a more tactical and thought-out flow of combat.  
  
That being said, I'd like to point out the vastly improved graphics when compared to POE1. Maps, character models, combat effects and textures: You name it and it's bound to look better, crisper and just more refined in this one. That also means that this game is a lot harder on your hardware. Not that it will melt your high-end CPU but you'd want a decent middle-tier gaming computer to run this game smoothly and, if you can, you should REALLY consider installing this game on an SSD drive as the loading times can be a bit annoying if the game runs on a conventional harddrive. Unfortunately, improved graphics come at a design price as the individual maps are much smaller in game-world scope. Many of the playable areas are city maps whaereas POE1 had those larger area maps which helped convey a sense of exploration. Whenever this games switches to the "exploring bits" it zoomes out to a world map view where many of the points of interest are then often presented as text-based roleplaying segments. That has the weird effect that an arguably larger game world can still feel smaller in comparison to POE1.  
  
There are also a couple of choices regarding game play which seem odd. High end item upgrades can be REALLY expensive, e.g. getting an item to legendary status costs 30k of your game currency (plus a bunch of rare materials). You can buy an entire new ship for that kind of money. Then there is the way spell books for mages work now which provide a selection of spells to which you add your learned spells from the leveling process. That's just weird and cumbersome compared to the little Pokemon-like mini game of "Gotta catch them all!" for spells your mage had in POE1. 
Skill checks are strange, too. There is this base skill + party support system in play here. Unfortunately, that isn't used consistently. Sometimes events check a companion skill and during other events you're stuck with your main characters skills and this selection can seem a little arbitrary.
Fortunately, we also see some improvements particularily in the character class system. There is a huge variety of playable characters as each class has several sub-classes and you can create multi-class charcters making for endless possibilities to design and play your hero with just the kind of playstyle you prefer and want which is supplemented by a great system for your party composition. You can create a party from scratch with new characters, giving you just the right kind of party composition you planned for. Then there are sidekicks which are like pre-rolled characters you meet during the game which often feature certain sub-classes not available in "normal" character creation and then there are "companions" who have their own particular background stories, motivations and side-missions. Companions even interact which eachother forming their own particular relations depending on how you choose to put them in your party. Some of these companions can even be romanced. These companions get their own story section in the game ending screen which can turn out vastly different depending on your interactions and game decisions.  
  
That leads me to the core feature of this game which is the narrative and story. Once again Obsidian really deliver here. Their story-telling crew must be among the most talented group of writers in the gaming industry. They really know their "tools of trade" as a complex net of quests are woven into an elaborate fabric of politics, intrigue and adventure. There are several factions in the game all competing with eachother. Sometimes even the factions have factions and those factions respond to your decisions, they influence your companions and the final outcome of your story. I think there only was one minor incident when my game choices lead to a small story inconsistency. Other than that the narrative execution was flawless. I wish other media had consistent writing like that (I'm looking at you "Game of Thrones" and "new Star Wars").  
Apart from these workman aspects of the story (which can really substract from the game if handled wrong) there is the overarching main story. Once again this part of the game is rather cerebral and philosophical. You can play this game as the "perfect knight" and still see the world evolve in a direction you might consider "bad" because people are diverse with different motivations and what you consider as "just&fair" might simply make it easier for the ruthless to exploit the weak. In essence this game is very philosophical leading you deep into the fogs of ethics and a constant weighing of alternatives between individual justice and the "greater good". A word of warning though: If you expect a classic "hero ending" then you might be very disappointed with this game. There is no "best ending". There might not even be an ending you wanted. You just get an ending reflecting your personal choices.  
  
Bottom line: A very deep and well-crafted RPG experience with only some minor game play peculiarities.

[h1]Boring and opaque[/h1]

Maybe I’m just getting old and jaded, but this doesn’t recapture the magic of the Infinity Engine games. After about forty hours I find myself struggling to stay interested.
What this game – and its predecessor – needs is a villain with a clear motivation and a setting you can understand without reading pages and pages and pages of exposition. I don’t remember Baldur’s Gate or even Planescape being this opaque, and I played those games when I was eleven.

It’s not even that the world of Deadfire isn’t, or can’t be, interesting. It’s a matter of presentation. Of finding ways to make the player immediately understand the stakes even if he doesn’t quite understand the world around him yet. Baldur’s Gate 2 did this with Irenicus: A mysterious mage who held you hostage and tortured you in a dark dungeon filled with sick experiments. Boom. Instant motivation to go after him and find out who he is and what he wants with you.

A rebellious god stomping across a continent can make for an interesting antagonist, but I need a reason to care. A reason that is presented to me upfront, not hidden away behind countless encyclopedia entries that I need to read in order to understand the game’s setting (seriously, I feel like half the text in a given dialogue is a blue link that leads me to some long-winded piece of exposition). I’m only ever told that I should go after Eothas, I never feel like it. Instead, I’m off doing side quests, which admittedly is fun for a while, but even that starts to become stale, because they’re not that interesting and a game of eternal side questing doesn’t have any stakes.

But maybe I’m focusing on the wrong thing, as I was told the meat of the game isn't in the story, but in the various factions you can join. And while they are kind of interesting, I’m honestly struggling to keep track of their names, ideals and how they stand in relation to each other. This, again, is down to their presentation. They are rarely shown to me in an organic way that lets me intuit who they are and what they’re about. The evil pirates are not seen doing evil pirate things, the imperialistic invaders don’t have a heavy and oppressive presence in the city streets. Rather, to learn about them, I need to go to each of their headquarters and talk to one of their sparsely characterized representatives so s/he can tell, tell, tell, tell me all about their philosophy, goals and history (in dialogue nodes with tons of blue links leading to yet more encyclopedia entries that I need to read to understand the context).
Contrast this with the factions in Baldur’s Gate 2. Did you need to exhaust several extensive dialogue trees to understand who the Cowled Wizards were? No, the second you tried casting a spell and they teleported out of nowhere and nuked you to oblivion, you knew all you needed to know about them. Characterization through in game events, rather than endless exposition.

If only the faction mechanics were robust, like in New Vegas, where building up a reputation with one faction inevitably meant alienating another, where being a legionnaire or an NCR ranger actually earned you staunch allies and terrible enemies. In my Deadfire playthrough I tried sucking up to the pirate faction, doing all their quests in the hope that the game would, you know, eventually treat me like a pirate, condemning me for murdering, pillaging and being an all-round asshole, but aside from a few throwaway lines here and there, no one seemed to care. I could still waltz into the headquarters of the trade federation – the pirates’ mortal enemies – and have a cup of coffee with their leader. It’s perfectly possible to achieve a maxed-out reputation with each faction, even if, logically, this shouldn’t be possible. This is because there’s little to no interplay between them. Rarely are you tasked with killing a certain NPC for the pirates and protecting that same NPC for the trade guys. And if you are, nothing much comes of it. At one point, the vile pirate king sent me to a remote island to slaughter a village of natives (who are a faction in and of themselves). The rest of the natives in the game didn’t care, but retained their friendly disposition towards me because I had once helped one of them retrieve his lost puppy.

The reputation system in general is wonky and weird. Why is it possible to build up a reputation for being both cruel [i]and[/i] benevolent at the same time? Why do all [cruel] and [aggressive] dialogue options boil down to being a cartoonishly evil roflvillain stealing children’s lunchboxes and threatening the elderly? Why does the game assume that if I choose a [benevolent] dialogue option, I’m actually being benevolent and not merely putting on a show to trick whoever I’m talking to? Why do all [stoic] dialogue options boil down to simply [saying nothing], even in situations where it makes no sense to keep quiet? Why are [clever] dialogue options always anything but? Why don’t [passionate] dialogue options let me choose what I’m passionate about? Why is it [rational] to surrender your gold and run away from a bunch of thugs you could handily wipe the floor with?
The main character’s dialogue choices are so poorly conceived and counterintuitive that I often wish I could choose none of them. I guess [saying nothing] isn’t such a bad choice after all.

It's a shame that Deadfire is plagued by such bad writing and design, because I like its beautiful, hand drawn backgrounds, its Caribbean inspired Deadfire Archipelago (a really cool and original setting for an RPG), the island hopping, the tomb diving, the massively improved itemization and even the combat (which was the first game’s biggest weakness), with its assortment of unique and hand placed encounters that are sure to be a challenge for even the most experienced cRPG afficionado.
Like many others, I would probably give Deadfire a mixed rating if Steam allowed it, but as it is, I can’t say I had enough fun with it to recommend it.

One of the best RPGs you will play, no doubt. 

I couldn't finish PoE 1 due to RtwP and immense text that it had and I don't regret it. This game however is fully voiced, I mean every freaking line, and is done so well it's actually fascinating. There are big names that does the voice acting like Laura Bailey, Ashley Johnson, Matthew Mercer and countless other ones. You will be amazed and in for a treat. 

Every decision matters. You will face the consequences of your choices and thus, choices have their own weight on your shoulders. That's why it's so immersive and made me play more than 160 hours without ever getting bored. Needed to do some lore refreshing to understand the motives of the Gods but it's easy to get into.
