You sail from island to island to create your own story and it is a wonderful idea. I wished the level cap was a little bit higher though as if you explored every part of the map, you will reach level 20 easily and won't gain a new level/ability etc. nearly 30% of the game. Mods increase the level cap from 20 to 33 but I didn't want to intervene.

DLCs in the game are fantastic as well, apart from one. Beast of Winter introduces a well made zone and character like Ydwin, plus the story behind it makes the main story more interesting. Seeker, Slayer, Survivor is the second DLC and focused around arena style combat and it's immensely boring. Boy, I cannot describe how boring it was as I decreased the difficulty to Story and breezed through fights so that they end more quickly. Utterly a pointless DLC that I wished I never experienced. The last one, however, is a spectacular DLC called The Forgotten Sanctum. It's mysterious and really intriguing with another connection to main story. I suggest you complete all DLCs before starting your last quest as they're filling the blanks, not adding more story to the ending. Also, last DLC adds 4 megabosses to the game that will literally destroy you. I certainly couldn't even stand the difficulty and killed all of them in Story mode while still struggling. No shame. :)

Initally wasn't planning on playing this game as well, however, they added Turn Based mode and it changed everything entirely. I mean the game basically become a different game and I think from now on, RtwP and Turn Based modes should be proposed to players no matter what. Each style has its advantages though. RtwP requires more awareness and certainly much much faster than Turn Based. Since the game initally created with the idea of RtwP, there are a lot of filler fights that becomes an instant chore on Turn Based. You can understand it from my playtime as well since some fights, which might have been a breeze with RtwP, takes nearly 30 minutes. Obsidian doesn't allow changing the modes in-game like Pathfinder does, so you need to use a console command to force the change if you want the RtwP mode back. They don't guarantee that you won't encounter any bugs, however it's better than nothing. Shame that I learned that 1 hour before the ending. Just write "SetTacticalMode Disabled" if you want RtwP back and "SetTacticalMode RoundBased" if you want it to be Turn Based. Easy for filler fights.

Also, as a completionist, I was happy to see the game's achievement system is built upon exploration, quests and easy collectibles. I wish every game developer approached completionism from this aspect since it makes you to explore and see the effort developers put. Easy and fun to achieve.

Game still has its problems though. Engine makes the performance complete shit and you feel it from the start. There's a huge stutter nearly every 10-16 seconds, memory leak problems and huge FPS drops due to CPU utilization. Basically if you have an older system, the game somehow works better. :) My rig is 9900K/RTX 3080 and couldn't get more than 80FPS in average. People report that it works better with older CPUs.

At the end, you get a summary of what you did in the game, the ramifications of your choices (which 100% changed the world and the future) and what happened to your companions. I don't feel ashamed to tell you that it really felt like saying goodbye to your friends and made me teary eyed. That is the result of wonderful voice acting, writing and the experience that the game gives you. Certainly recommended.

It's taken me a long time to figure out what I feel about the Pillars Of Eternity games. The first one was rougher in so many ways, and I thought I hated it. The second one, this one, Deadfire, I thought I hated, too.

But with both of them, I just kept playing for some reason. All the way to the end. Multiple times. And then I realized that really, it's not that I hated them, it's that I wasn't really seeing them. I was seeing what I was projecting onto them.

Deadfire is the (slightly) larger of the two and most recent, so I'll put the review here, but the first one really is a masterpiece in its own right (ragged edges inherited from clumsy D&D paradigms and all). Both games benefit tremendously from a few judiciously chosen mods to either polish or expand or balance certain little things.

Mechanically, if there were ever a spiritual successor of the famous Infinity Engine RPGs like Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale or the Electron / Aurora Engine NWN, it must be Pillars Of Eternity. Which should surprise no one, given the lineage of the designers and direct references.  Absolutely luscious, gorgeous environments, tactical combat with just enough complexity and depth to be tactical, and a good basketful of companions to take with you, both games are the perfect archetypes of classical western RPGs. No one could say they have a right to comment about the RPG genre without having played these two.

And so now I'm gonna give critical comments about them.

Although the companions are diverse and usually have compelling personal stories and interesting or attractive personalities, they (almost all) suffer from a crippling problem: they're extremely "safe". They tell boringly predictable stories about tediously superficial drama and your relationship with them resembles nothing quite so much as being their unpaid therapist. This is a problem born of the demands of corporate-governed game design, and it's just tragic. Thus, the companions come across as shallow Saturday morning cartoons for tweens. For one example, Tekehu is an obnoxiously blunt token hypersexual himbo whose story mostly revolves around his privileged immaturity... but his confrontation with the exhaustively-demonstrated injustices of his culture consists of approximately three lines of dialogue in which he mopes that he wants you to hug him. So brave. A man asking for a hug. Such radical progress. What an amazingly non-toxic masculine - NO, he actually is just a shallow slut dumping his insecurities onto you and requires you to tell him what to think about it all. After a short exchange of melodramatic navel gazing and clumsy, rushed pleas to be your lover. Eder's major foible is that he's supposed to be "racist". Not racist like ... *racist* though. No no no. That would be too much. He's "racist" with quotation marks because he wants to pet the Orlans like he pets literally anything smaller and hairier than he is, and sometimes he says so and ohhhh isn't that super awkward and racist you guys?! Woooooow... If he were allowed to be portrayed as unlikeable or hateful somehow, that would be a line too far for the game's main character. Yes, Eder is the main character.

This pattern is one demonstrated through virtually every dialogue interaction. Your companions just can't help themselves but to constant provide vapid one-liners and trivial interjections begging for a giggle that's almost never deserved. Why? Because any sincere humor would be risky. The horror is mostly just a muddy old ruin where there's some stinky piles of poop laying around. There is one dungeon that attempts to really go all the way, showing how the lives of the underclass ~~slaves~~ workers rot in heaps where they were disposed in the dank bowels beneath the city. But this is not really a point ever remarked upon or brought up elsewhere. You see the environment, but it may as well just be a random undead-themed dungeon. Once you emerge from that place, none of your companions ever talk about it. There's a token throwaway comment about it in one dialogue when turning in the quest and that's about it. When you go to the island where the ~~slave~~trade is being conducted, this shrieking silence continues. The game obviously wanted to confront the ugliness and realities of colonial-era labor rights and industrialization, but absolutely and completely failed to do so. Except for the technicality that the plot designers took care to point out that no one in the Deadfire is actually "the good guys". But that was a perfunctory, bare minimum. The overall moral of this fable about the responsibility of divinity is handled in such abstract terms that it actually fails to have emotional impact because even the few moments during which the player is confronted by this plot point are presented in such a casual, nonchalant manner.

If you are able to understand the constraints placed upon a work of art like this by the accountants and executives at Obsidian, you can probably forgive them for not really exploring these things in the depth they would need. For one thing, it'd be rather expensive. The plot could easily sprawl far beyond its scope just to discuss and illustrate those things (the Watcher is able to subvert and weaken certain factions in some ways, but leading a revolution to liberate the oppressed and exploited slave-caste of Neketaka, for example, is just not possible).

Similarly, if you can overlook the now-well-examined frustrations of ancient D&D game design mechanics (Vancian spellcasting, I'm looking at you...), or if you can install a few mods to help alleviate the most egregious problems, you can fairly well enjoy the tactical combat while also having an immersive fantasy life experience. The multiple difficulty settings allow you a great deal of power to determine the degree and type of difficulties you face.

Perhaps the only fault that truly is the responsibility of the game developers (rather than their managers, marketers and financiers) is that the character models are... ugly. Especially if you want to wear robes.

Last notes: don't use the turn-based mode. It was added eventually just to satisfy some loud, toxic voices of their playerbase. Mechanically, it is absolutely not balanced (since the fundamental design of your action economy being affected by your choice of equipment just goes out the window), and is simply not necessary, either. And use a mod to get rid of the absolutely stupid non-party-friendly AoEs. Yes that will make you "more powerful", but in practice it's only a quality of life improvement.

These many years later, the Pillars Of Eternity games are both masterpieces of their genre, only surpassed by the more modern Pathfinder games by Owlcat.

Turn-based mode saved this game for me.

My passion for fantasy games was fostered by a game called Temple of Elemental Evil made by Troika Games, and I have installed that game on every single PC I've ever owned. There was something so special about creating an entire adventuring band of heroes, and setting off into the Moat House that I must have done it a hundred times. Alas, there is only so many times you can play a single game before you want the rush of a new experience, and I tried a bunch of the classic isometric RPGs from the era, and some spiritual successors (including Pillars of Eternity I); nothing was the same.  The uncontrolled chaos, inability to execute your plan to perfection, and the simplistic allied AI that would take over when you couldn't be bothered to babysit them had me closing the game, wanting more almost every time 3-4 hours in.

Pillars of Eternity II changed that for me with this update. I purchased this game a long time ago, and it sat at 4 hours total, and 1 hour of in-game time until that ballooned into over 100+ hours in the past month. It's fantastic, and well worth the money, but not without flaws.

This game was not designed from the ground up with turn based in mind as say Divinity: Original Sin II, and there are obviously some kinks in that chain. For example, Dexterity is mostly a useless stat since it would increase your action speed in Real-Time with Pause. That could essentially give you x2, x4, or more attacks than a slower enemy. Now, it only controls your location in the queue for the next round. You cannot, to my knowledge, stack initiative that you may act twice in a single round. 

With that being said, I can not put this game down. The characters are written quite well, and the languages spoken by some truly add to the experience of being a scurvy sailor forging their own path in a relatively unexplored island chain. Each time I came across a new island, I got a rush of excitement, and I couldn't wait to explore the ancient ruin filled with secrets (and often an interesting item), the new town I was supposed to find much later in my adventure, or the hideout of a strong, and fearsome creature waiting to be put down, and plundered like the pirate captain I was.

I don't write reviews often, and I apologize if this does not contain a comprehensive list of pros, and cons of the title, however, in my personal opinion, if you enjoy RPGs, and you enjoy pirates, you can not miss the opportunity to add this to your library.

Looking forward to another game or two using this system.  A winner in my book.

[h1]In-Depth[/h1]
[h3]Divided We Stand[/h3]
Caed Nua lies in ruins, the Watcher's soul once again is split by the return of Eothas, now marching through the Deadfire Archipelago for reasons yet unknown. Resurrected as the herald of Berath, God of death, you'll have to chase the rogue deity and stop whatever plans he has in mind. The Deadfire is home to a conspicuous Aumaua population, however far from united: rivaling factions and tribes often walk the line between tolerance and conflict. For this reason, the Adra-rich islands are exploited by many factions from all over Eora, each trying to harness the magical green substance for their own interest. 

Rich in lore and superbly written in all departments, this setting delivers the depth expected from a Pillars game: from companions to quests and books found all over, there rarely is a dull moment for knowledge-thirsty players. Story-wise, expect a multi-faceted plot that blurs the lines between good and evil, with several in-between options as far as choices and alliances go. 

[h3]Choice & Consequence[/h3]
Each major outpost or point of interest is often home to quests, tasks and plentiful roleplaying interactions. Depending on your character and party members' skills, a variety of options open up to solve most situations, ranging from diplomacy, intimidation, guile to old-fashioned combat. Hand-drawn panels are especially common during exploration and secondary locations: they act as small, standalone text-based RPGs that make excellent use of your party's skills as a whole, with meaningful and exciting consequences for both failures and successes. Whatever the situation may be, you can be sure PoE2 will give you not one but many choices, and it will be up to you to make the best of them... with tangible consequences.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2754619390

[h3]The Pirate's Life is for Me![/h3]
You'll be able to use your very own vessel to sail across the Deadfire, and manage many aspects such as crew roles, provisions, armament and upgrades. Each of these changes will be reflected in the numerous interactions with other sailors, the crew and the many challenges the sea itself presents.  Feeding your men cheap hardtack and bland water will result in moral loss, same goes for harshly treating the crew or surrendering to an enemy vessel - fail enough, and you'll have a mutiny on your hands. Conversely, a happy crew will function better and be ready to face even the most tumultuous situations. 

Naval battles are another highlight: they play out as text-based interactions between ships, where you'll commandeer the vessel's direction, speed, cannons and crew to try and sink the enemy. Depending on your sailors' experience, assignments and the vessel's armaments / equipment, different approaches to combat come into play. A weaker vessel may win by boarding the enemy ship and solve the matter with traditional combat, as a weaker crew could win by superiority of equipment. The conceited screams of battle, thundering of cannons and reasonable depth of mechanics make naval battles exciting and a good change of pace, however the enemy AI isn't too bright most of the time. Weaker ships can win against far superior vessels with the right maneuvering... since the enemy won't use the full potential of what they have.

[h3]The Art of Battle[/h3]
Combat can be either traditional real-time with pause, or turn-based as an optional mode. This latter one kinda breaks the balance of several skills and builds, and makes battles drag on much further; I recommend the regular mode. That being said, combat in PoE2 pits up to five team members against greatly varied foes, ranging from undead, constructs, wild animals and spirits to vampires and cursed abominations. The sheer variety of enemies, most of which have unique behaviors, skills and attributes, makes combat always interesting even after dozens of hours. Party composition has never been more flexible, thanks to the multi-class system that allows combining any two specializations to create potent hybrids, at the price of slower leveling, though. 

An all-new behavior editor is present, allowing custom configuration of each companion's AI with custom rules and conditions - on paper a great system... that however won't work that well in many occasions. I found the good old "micromanage everything yourself" way the best one, especially on higher difficulties where even a single mistake can mean death. The usual PoE variety of equipment, skills, spells and abilities of all kinds is present, even more varied and rich than in the first entry: there truly is no limit to what you can build yourself and your party into. Generally on Veteran and POTD difficulties combat is challenging at all times, while the brutally unfair (thankfully optional) Mega Bosses will test the limits of your strategy with epic fights you won't forget (or overcome) easily. Those who love tactical RPG fighting need to look no further.

This is a must-play for any CRPG fan. The story and combat are amazing (in turn-based mode). The writing is top-notch. The character systems: chef's kiss. And the world building is one of the best of any rpg franchise. 

My only complaint is that the level cap is too low. I hit it when I had only finished 1 out of 3 expansions, and I had only explored about 75% of the map. I think I easily had another 100 hours left. But as you approach level 20, and definitely after you hit it, there's absolutely no point in exploring or fighting further. Progression becomes 0, as, due to the upgrade system, getting new loot becomes pointless too. 

Thankfully, the plot of the main quest is spectacular (if very short), so after I hit the level cap, I just plowed the last bit of the main quest, and enjoyed it like one would enjoy reading a good book -- by that point my party was insanely overpowered, so the last few fight were hilariously easy.

Don't let any of this dissuade you from trying out what is otherwise a top tier CRPG. I spent a 102 hours on it, and I loved every minute. That's a good purchase no matter how much you pay for it. 99%, I'll replay it in the future and do the other two expansions too.

Oh and a bit of advice: The ship management is bullshit, invest all of your wealth in your party, and just board everyone. The ship combat sucks, anyway.

Pillars of Eternity 2 is a D&D style RPG where the player controls a party of characters in pauseable real time combat. The story takes place after the events of the first PoE game, as the Watcher and their companions pursue a God who threatens the island chain known as the Deadfire archipelago. 

The Good

-	Combat system will be instantly familiar to anyone who played PoE, or other RPGs like Baldur’s Gate and Dragon Age.
-	Magic spells, which had limited uses in the previous game, now refresh after every encounter. This means you can cast your most powerful spells in every fight, rather than saving them for a difficult encounter, which makes the combat more exciting (although perhaps easier).
-	PoE’s unusual health system, where you could only fully heal by resting, has been removed in favour of a traditional system. This makes me happy, because my main character is usually a Cleric/Priest, and in Deadfire I can actually heal my party.
-	Each companion has their own personal quest involving characters from their past, or organisations that they’re loyal to. They feel like they have a purpose in the world, and they don’t just exist to blindly serve the player character. If they don’t like your choices, they might even leave your party.
-	The player character is silent, but every NPC who is involved in a quest is fully voiced. Less reading! \o/
-	Voice acting is fantastic all around, especially for the companions, but I need to give a special mention for Laura Bailey, Ashley Johnson and Matthew Mercer, because they’re always amazing, and everybody should know who they are (seriously, look them up on IMDB).
-	Quests often have multiple solutions, and don’t always need to result in violence. Non combat skills such as diplomacy, intimidate and bluff will frequently give you more dialogue options.
-	Some quests will allow you to choose which side of a conflict to support, and its not always easy to choose, because there aren’t really any obvious “these are the good guys!” factions. My big main quest choice came down to a process of elimination of who I thought was least bad.
-	As the setting for Deadfire is a group of islands, you’ll travel around the world map by sailing your own ship. You can recruit a crew and will need to make sure you’ve got enough food and drink to keep them alive, and enough money to pay their wages. If you wanted to ignore the main quest, you could probably entertain yourself for hours by roleplaying as a pirate.
-	It took me 45 hours to finish the main quest and some side quests, which represents good value for money.
-	I didn’t suffer any bugs or crashes.
-	The music is excellent, including the sea shanties that your crew will sometimes sing as you sail around the world map.

The Bad

-	Party size has been reduced from six to five. It doesn’t make the combat more difficult, but it does make it harder to decide which companions to bring along. There are nine companions to recruit, including three returning favourites from the first game, and I wanted to use three others frequently for story/quest reasons, but I always had to leave two of these six behind. And this also forced me to pretty much ignore three others.
-	I felt that too many lines of dialogue include made up foreign language words which you then have to hover the mouse pointer over to get a translation so you can properly understand the context. Think of a French character saying “Oui” instead of “Yes”, but then also apply the same mechanic to a dozen other words like no, thanks, sorry, swear words, job titles, etc. I shouldn’t need to learn a foreign language to properly understand a story.
-	You can engage in naval combat against other ships, but this plays out through a turn based mini game, which might be the weakest part of Deadfire. I tried to avoid it as much as possible. And when I couldn’t avoid it, I just gave orders to close the distance so that I could board the enemy ship and have a normal combat encounter.
-	The world map sometimes gave me the same feeling as an open world game (one of the bad ones by Ubisoft), filled with so much inconsequential stuff. Having dozens of side quests, being able to travel in any direction at any time, and the presence of many smaller islands which can be explored for loot and resources, can have a negative effect on the pacing of the story, especially in the first half of the game.
-	The final section of the story was a huge anticlimax, its difficult to explain why without spoilers, but I felt like my involvement in the main quest was ultimately irrelevant.
-	You can’t continue with unfinished side quests after completing the main quest, because the game is over. I suspected this would be the case because the previous game did the same thing, but I still don’t like it. Especially because characters talk about the main quest with a “the world might end” sense of urgency, so it doesn’t make sense for a player who wants to do every quest to be like “yeah, well, that God can wait until I’ve finished hunting down these random bounties”.

The Recommendation

While not as great as I hoped it would be, if you enjoyed playing the first Pillars of Eternity, or RPGs in general, you should mostly enjoy Deadfire. I would advise playing the previous game first, to gain a better understanding of the story, characters, and world events.

I have genuinely tried to not even love, but at least like this game. The first one was incredible, thick with atmosphere, introducing a fascinationg world, dark, somehow new, filled with memorable characters and an amazing questlines. I enjoyed every minute of it, went back to play it again and again. But Deadfire? After spending 85 hours exploring it I just... stopped. Couldn't force myself to play anymore, couldn't be bothered about almost anything. And I couldn't wrap my head around why exactly that happened. I'm a seasoned RPG player, I loved the first game, what was wrong? 
And I think my answer would be a mix of atmosphere, tedious mechanics and the game just being too big and too empty. And sadly, the writing. 

First, the atmosphere. It was... not what I expected after the first game. The murky, cold Dyrwood with celtic-inspired language, folklore and rather dark history was something I instantly fell in love with. The hollow children, the bloody cults, the entire deal with animancy... it was fascinating, sometimes oppressive, sometimes chilling. With a villain I was both afraid of and intrigued by. White March took us farther north, offered something else, but bringing back the nice memories of Icewind Dale. And Deadfire? Well... Carribean-like setting, pirates, sea battles and very political commentary about colonialism was not what I expected. At all. I tried to be open minded, but it just felt... off, like somebody took all that darkness and eerieness and replaced it with something lighter and more adventurous. Not my cup of tea. 

Second, the mechanics and the open world. Okay, the concept was neat. Your own ship, hiring your own crew and exploring the map with many hidden places, even undiscovered islands you could name yourself. I loved it for the first 20 hours, not gonna lie... but then it turns into a chore. If you're the type of player who likes to explore everything, my condolences, you have hours of boring, repetitive and honestly tedious sailing minigame before you. The map is massive, you have to manage resources to keep the crew's morale high enough, but the worst part is that most of the time what you find around the world is not even that rewarding. After hours of clicking around the world map you click some more around a dusty scrap of land with a single dungeon on it. Or get a quest if you're lucky. The sea battles minigame is... ugh, not very fun. You either board the enemy ship, sustaining some damage to your own vessel, or play an annoying text-based battle with a lot of math. Needless to say, I wasn't a fan. 

And last but not least - the writing. It was... weird. The tone was completely different from the previous game, a bit of political commentary about colonnialism and cultural clash of various nations. Also, factions, a lot of factions with unclear agendas playing a local game of power. Again, sounds nice, but I found the storyline simply hard to follow. Who wanted what, who had what opinions on who, why were my companions upset about me talking to someone, who are all these people. To understand it, you need to read a lot of exposition - way too much. And that comes from someone who usually snorts every single bit of lore like cocaine. I was bored. I didn't get why should I care about any of these factions and if they were even a part of the main story or not. Two years after playing the last time, I can't remember a single thing, nothing sticks. I tried to load the save, hoping I would remember anything and... nothing. Not a single thing. 
Characters were another problem. Somehow the people I loved in the first game seemed so different in the second one, and there seemed to be less interactions with them. The reputation system was neat, and some of their banter was funny, but most of the time it felt like they hated each other. And - in my opinion - the best written character, Ydwin, didn't even make it to the game as a full companion. She is the only reason I still decided to try to finish the game. 

There were good things too - it's a well-made game, technically works great, fighting system was upgraded, graphics and sound are still fantastic, but the three things I wrote about just ruined the whole thing for me. Slowly, steadily, they turned the game into a chore instead of a fun way to spend my evenings. If you're looking for something similar to the first game - don't play it, it's completely different. If you're looking for something new, unique and don't mind a lot of politics or exploration of a bit empty world - go for it. 
It just wasn't for me.

This sequel brings even a ship and a crew for you to give form and manage at ease. Overall, [b]a massive canvas to define [u]your own[/u] story and personality[/b].

Pathfinder: WOTR left the bar very high for me (I'm spoiled), but Pillars Of Eternity: Deadfire is everything you want on an RPG.

+ The companions are nice. Eder, Aloth and Pellegina are back, which is nice. Especially Eder and Aloth, who I always take along. However, you can't make everybody happy and some may leave your party (more on this later.)

I just finished Pillars of Eternity II: Deadfire and it was a good game, but it wasn't a great game and I can definitely understand the less than stellar reaction and sales. 

In hindsight, the team should have known that following up on the original's success would be a tall order. It was essentially a remake of Baldur's Gate II in many ways, and it hit all the right tones and strengths of the game it drew inspiration from. And this, I think is what complicated things. You see, the classic Baldur's Gate II does not, so far, have a successor that has come to surpass it, not even its own proper sequel. It's certainly not perfect and I wouldn't consider it one of those lightning in a bottle games that just did everything right in a way that can not be repeated, but that achievement has not yet been reached. And Deadfire was an attempt at reaching it.

In trying to do so, the developers seem to have leaned far too much into the strengths of another contemporary game that seemed to fare commercially very well for itself: Divinity Original Sin. Every idea in Deadfire that seemed to be borrowed from that game felt out of place and poorly executed. The turn based mode, introduced post-launch as an experiment for the original game, simply does not make the game more enjoyable, and the real-time with pause experience has suffered significantly from what seems to be a problem of a small team trying to balance two completely unrelated game modes against each other. Yet, at the end of the day where Deadfire fell flat most for me was the writing.

Chasing a god across a dangerous archipelago in a ship with eccentric and esoteric companions sounds like a great idea for a fantasy novel but it really does not translate to the interactive medium well. At least in this attempt. I mean, it does have its merits - I loved how every single faction you can ally with are downright evil bastards in some way and how every faction quest pretty much results in the slaughter and suffering of hundreds to thousands of innocent people. In that regard, it conveys the complicated political and moral situation in Deadfire very well. What it doesn't do is to make it interesting and fun. There are two things severely lacking in this writing that turned me sour quickly and I never really recovered that interest: 1. There is no urgency, 2. There is no agency. At the end of the day Eothas sat on a mysterious island waiting for almost a year for me to arrive while I was having my jolly old time sailing across the seas and grinding for gear and experience. That kind of gameplay does not mesh well with this kind of story, no.

The ultimate downer for me was that after hoing the game would redeem itself all the way until the final confrontation, it ended with me having zero agency with regards to the main plot. Sure, I made dozens of decisions which resulted in end game slides and caused all kinds of things in many parts of the setting, but the main story basically resolved itself with my decision affecting the outcome even less so than picking a color at the end of Mass Effect 3. For that, I feel cheated. The final DLC for this game, The Forgotten Sanctum, is a 20-25 hour long high level and self contained campaign that has better writing, better urgency, better agency and a more satisfying ending than the whole game - that alone tells you something was missing with the original.

All in all, it was a sad farewell to Eder, Pallegina and Aloth. There were some very memorable new NPCs, and Maia will forever be the best waifu, and I will miss them all a lot. A third game in this series seems to be a very long shot after the poor sales of Deadfire, but one can hope.. All in all, I will recommend this game if you were a fan of the original, but Tyranny was better.

One night, several years after the events of the original Pillars of Eternity, the keep of Caed Nua erupts. From the catacombs below, the colossal adra sculpture that had previously lain inanimate hefts itself up from its tomb of dirt. In the wake of its emergence the keep is rendered to ruin, its inhabitants dead and their souls taken by the pilfered by the giant. Eothas, god of light and rebirth, has been reborn into to the mortal world and embodied himself within the monolithic crystal sculpture. He marches fort, uncaring, driven with unknown intent, wreaking death and destruction in his wake.

Tasked by the Goddess Berath to trail Eothas, you track him to the Deadfire Archipelago, an island cluster squirming under a three-way tussle of political and naval powers; The Vailian Trading Company have muscled into the Deadfire to study and mine its unique Adra resources. The Rauataian government and their Royal Deadfire Company lay claim to the Deadfire Archipelago and wish to ensure both the safety of their people and stability within the Deadfire. Finally, the Príncipi sen Patrena are a loosely connected and regulated organisation of pirates that terrorise the surrounding seas. The ruinous passing of Eothas enflames the tension between these factions, and while they pester you to resolve the issue, they also see an opportunity to use you for their own ends.

The story in Pillars of Eternity 2 is set on a much grander scale than the previous game, and while it could be played as a standalone without much issue, it very much builds on the story framework of events and revelations of the first game. The story of the first game did the arduous (and at times somewhat overwhelming) busy work of revealing the history of the world, freeing the sequel to be bolder in its approach. The result is that your objective in Pillars of Eternity 2 is clear and evident from the start, which is a wonderful change from the vague wandering and slow reveal of the previous game. Here, you know what you need to do – it’s how you go about doing it that matters. This freedom allows the game to explore the world and flesh it out, which goes hand in hand with its emphasis on exploration.

Your choices in the first game do carry over to the sequel, and affect how some people choose to speak with you, and how they view you. You can load a save, but you can also answer some questions if you’d prefer to tailor your results or if you simply haven’t played the first game. The character you play as has no bearing on if you load a save or not, allowing you to create a completely new character, rather than getting stuck with your original class.

Speaking of story, one of the very first things one notices about the sequel as the introductory narration begins is the astounding voice acting. The vast majority of the conversations you have are fully voice acted, but special praise should be given to the voice of the narrator as she describes the more important story moments. The voice is wonderfully evocative, both wistful and passionate, as it describes the events unfolding.

The cinematic visuals are almost always static, as they were in the first game, but are now also beautifully illustrated, with wonderful and fantastical use of colour. The writing is fantastically descriptive and evocative, allowing one to feel fully immersed in the moment. All of these combine to create a dream-like narrative experience reminiscent of storybooks being read to one as a child, your eyes wide as your imagination blooms in wonder.

The wonderful moments of background character interactions are back as well, which are gold for humour or subtle character depth. One of my favourite moments in the first game involved Edér interacting with Sagani’s wolf, and I was overjoyed to see that quietly touched on with the animal companion of one of the new characters.

Quite a few mechanics have been improved and polished, the most immediate example being when one levels characters. Whereas in the first game one had to browse through lists when choosing new abilities for characters, there’s now a skill tree that, while mechanically similar, allows for far greater ease in browsing one’s choices. When travelling to locations, upon reaching it you can often choose to warp directly to one of the places of interest you’ve already discovered within that location.

As for new content, characters care about each other far more now. The character personalities are far stronger, and the game is far more comfortable at throwing characters at you that you may strongly dislike off the bat, and the rest of your party will react to them as well. Conflicting views over religion, behaviour, or acts of skulduggery can eventually result in outright arguments between party members that you have to resolve.

Characters can grow great affection for one another as well, in ways that can potentially shift their own worldview. How they treat you, and how they treat others, are also largely influenced by how you choose to resolve situations. Choosing duty and professionalism may impress one party member to like you more, whereas one who sees more value in deceit and selfishness will be disappointed in you.

The way that combat mechanics have evolved is also very interesting. The maximum health of characters now only drops when a character is knocked out, and three knockouts are potentially fatal. Spells and abilities are now refreshed after each encounter, rather than having to use campfires or Inns to regain them, and in fact, campfires are no longer a mechanic at all, as food can be given to party members to allow them to recover. The overall combat and damage system feels considerably smoother as a result, allowing for further forays into dungeons without having to break it up with returns to safe havens or expending limited campfire supplies. Beyond that, combat is largely the same: real-time combat that you can pause to issue orders, with cool downs in between every character action. Reacting to situations quickly is still immensely important, and learning to read and respond to the environment is crucial – the real-time nature of the game can easily result in a character dying astonishingly quickly if you’re not paying attention, and threats can often only be evident after it’s far too late.

Exploration is now hugely expanded, something that’s immediately obvious near the start of the game. Rather than having a map with places that you can fast travel to, you now move around the map itself, exploring places of interest. Many of this are just areas where you can collect food and water for your ship (more about this in a bit), some are narrative encounters where you can find some equipment or some foes to fight, and some are dungeons hidden away. While the individual islands may be small, the naval map itself is immense in size, so much so that exploring it all may seem daunting at first. The island cities have their own map showing the various districts, and there’s the chance you may encounter events as you travel between districts.

Your ship is what you’ll be using to get to these islands, another new mechanic the game provides. Your crew need pay, but also food and water to keep morale up, giving sudden importance to all the food one and drinks one finds lying about. There’s a fair bit of trial by fire when it comes to ship combat and exploration, though – while the game flings tutorials at you, it’s another thing to remember everything in the deluge of information, and it will take a few moments until you learn and understand how things work.

Pillars of Eternity 2: Deadfire improves upon the Pillars of Eternity formula in nearly every way and is another fine RPG from Obsidian, brilliantly showcasing the studio’s knack for strong world-building, intelligent, expressive writing, and varied quest design. If you play it you’ll discover one of the deepest, densest and most rewarding RPG.

The POE series is really great for those of us who were looking for a successor to the Baldur's Gate/Icewind Dale games. While there are a couple of other attempts at scratching the nostalgia itch of the old Infinity Engine games, POE is the only series that comes close to doing that. I can't understand why this one wasn't a financial success. They certainly went in a different direction with the whole sailing/pirates theme and it took some getting used to but I eventually learned to like it. It still has the same "feel" of an IE game. Immersion and dialogue are obviously super important in an RPG and I feel like POE does it fairly well, especially in comparison to another similar game from another studio that totally fails in this regard. In fact, I wish some of the sidekicks had been full companions with more dialogue as I felt that they could have been really interesting. In particular, Mirke, Rekke and Ydwin had a lot of unused potential. Unfortunately, it doesn't look like there is going to be a POE3, which sucks because I wanted more from these characters.

My main complaint about Deadfire is the same as in the original POE: I found the POE pantheon to be rather underwhelming. The gods/goddesses just seem like idiots. Their behavior is absolutely absurd. By contrast, the Forgotten Realms pantheon was much better. The "good/lawful gods" felt like powerful forces of justice. The evil gods felt like entities that should be feared. In POE, over the entire series, I felt like, "hey. I could do the whole divine being thing a lot better than any of these clowns."

Another minor point is one that I think gets overlooked because it is something that most people only pick up on subconsciously and that is music and sound. Both POE games go a little bit too heavy on the music and not enough on the ambient sounds. Icewind Dale is the perfect example of how to do sound correctly in an RPG. There is more emphasis on things like the howling of the wind and the crunching of the snow beneath your feet. Other IE games emphasize the sounds of the city or the birds in the trees. You feel immersed in the environment rather than a repetitive music track. Again, this is a minor point but one that I believe creates for better immersion.

All in all, POE is a good attempt at recreating what the fans love about games like BG/IWD and PS:T. I wish that more games like this would be made. I hope that fans of the old games are not being forgotten about. I feel like Baldur's Gate 3 is catering more towards fans of Larian/Divinity than those that are looking for the nostalgia of the old Baldur's Gate games. Maybe there can be a reboot of something like POE.

The game of thrones of cRPGS in both good and bad. Ambitious, well written, fantastic plot points and themes. Combat and character creation is fantastic and among the best of any RPG. The story, setting and plot make other RPGs look silly and immature in comparison. Despite all of these positives, the game does have glaring issues. 

The pacing is questionable, the plot lines are too intertwined and are an absolute mess in terms of gameplay. There is too much busy work and content bloat that could be trimmed down. The UI is awful and real time with pause is clunky, causing combat on higher difficulties to take forever and require more micromanagement than the original Baldur's gate. The scale and setting gets too big and convoluted at times and it really does hurt the gameplay experience.

Overall the game is fantastic but I highly recommend not playing on higher difficulties until after multiple playthroughs. Understanding the story, combat, item and  plot progression would take 2-3 playthroughs and if you're first timing the game on POTD or veteran it is likely to become an enormous slog at the end. Really only recommend POTD if you are truly in love with the game and have a deep understanding of its mechanics. Not because it's insanely difficult, but that it would take an enormous amount of time to complete a playthrough without an indepth knowledge of the game.
BG3 is good but falls off hard halfway through; PoE2 doesn't have the highs of BG3, but is a much more solid experience throughout.  This game deserves a bigger audience.

And there are a million different buffs and debuffs in this game, but sometimes you cannot see what they are or what they do, it's really frustrating.
Let's not even talk about the text based boat combat. Just ignore that part of the game.
The companions are interesting and have very good voice acting. The reputation system is nice. In general the writing is fantastic and the banter can be hilarious. I'm very happy the option to have romances is there but it's quite underwhelming. 
The character customization has no limits and you can do some cool builds. 
The story itself is intriguing but you get slapped in the face about colonialism and capitalism around every corner and it's just exhausting tbh. If you love politics, this game is for you.

[h1]“Why is the rum gone?!!”
[i]~Captain Jack Sparrow[/i][/h1]

[b]Obsidian Entertainment[/b]. It's hard not to love them, right? I mean, the guys are, like, our last hope for some good old school [b]RPG[/b]s nowadays. And yet... sometimes they make totally noobish mistakes. But I think I'll return to it a bit later. Because the main idea about this game? It's awesome. Simple like that. Absolutely... completely... [i]awesome![/i] I mean, what was wrong with the original [b]Pillars of Eternity[/b]? Well, two things actually. First – it was an obvious [b]Baldur's Gate[/b] clone and second – it had too much lore that... was pretty hard to care about. Can't say they've fixed the second problem here. The game still comes with tons and tons of stuff that you'll need to learn and... you know how it is.

When it's about huge settings like [b]Forgotten Realms[/b] or [b]Warhammer[/b], you [i]do[/i] want to learn about stuff. Just because there are many ways to interact with those worlds outside video games. By learning about the lore, you'll be able to read books, comics and, obviously, play the extremely fun tabletop games with your friends. You don't just [i]learn[/i] about those worlds. You live and breath them. For example, I still remember having that friend who started playing [b]Baldur's Gate[/b] without knowing a thing about the lore. He asked me who's that [b]Drizzt[/b] guy and why's he so important and I was, like, “[i]Order some pizza, man, it'll take time![/i]”. Now, imagine learning all that just... to play two video games. And it's not like learning process will be any fun here either. It'll be just history, gods, tribes, names, whatever else there is... again and again with no end. The game just keeps throwing names on you and expecting you to care. It doesn't work that way! So, like I said, they totally didn't fix the second problem of the first game.

The first one, though? They've annihilated it. With passion. Even though the game still has quite a lot of stuff taken directly from [b]Baldur's Gate[/b], it [i]does[/i] feel fresh now. Why? Well, because... the new game comes with... pirates. Yes, pirates. In [b]Pillars of Eternity[/b] you'll get your own ship, you'll get your own crew of drunk a-holes, you'll sail the seas and you'll search for the answer to the ultimate question of all times - how much wood could a woodchuck chuck if a woodchuck could chuck wood? Jokes aside, though, [b]Pillars of Eternity[/b] took the exploration from [b]Sid Meier's Pirates[/b], added naval battles from [b]Konung 2: Blood of Titans[/b] and put [b]Baldur's Gate[/b] on top of all that. Sounds incredible, right? [i]Right?[/i]

Well, unfortunately, it's time for us to remember what I've said at the beginning of this review. Sometimes, [b]Obsidian[/b] can make some noobish mistakes. And this game suffers from one of the most common noobish mistakes of them all. Developers here had a lot of ambitions. Like... [i]a lot[/i] of them. But clearly, they didn't have enough power behind them to turn those ambitions into reality. And right after the initial “WOW!” effect from ship management and naval battles disappears, you begin to see [b]Pillars of Eternity 2[/b] for what it is. And what it is... is..... well...... let's just say that this game is far from being a masterpiece. For many reasons.

My biggest complain here is technical difficulties. I mean, [b]Obsidian[/b]'s games are known to be buggy as heck, but this game? It's on the whole new level. Regular bugs aside (even though yes, we still have them, deal with it), it's... a technical disaster, really. Not only it'll freeze when you'll choose certain dialogue options (yes, even after years of updates), sometimes... the game won't even start at all. Yes, for real. The black screen bug is one of the most frustrating and annoying things here. It's just that. You pay for a game... and it won't even start. Have a nice day. Like... [i]what the heck?![/i] It's a really sad thing to see and I totally fail to understand why did they waste so much time on extra stuff like optional turn-based battle mode (pretty interesting addition, though), while the game itself barely works up to this day. It's like your roof is leaking, but you're wasting your on your action figures. But even if we'll forget about the technical details, the game is still... not nearly as good as you'll want it to be.

To begin with, the world, despite being pretty big, is quite empty here. And even though I totally loved the fact that we'll be able to discover and name the new islands, very often those islands have close to nothing on them. It's just that – you'll just sale around, looking for... nothing. Very soon exploration will start feeling like a boring routine. A naval battle here, a giant boss there, an optional dungeon, some resources... But nothing [i]really[/i] interesting. And guess what? There's another thing that makes exploration to feel even worse.

I'm talking, of course, about your crew. I'll tell you what - it'll require a lot of attention. [i]A lot[/i] of it. The suckers will require both food and water on daily basis (you'll always need to have enough of those with you), they'll have a morale meter (make sure to buy them some expensive things, share money with them and so on, otherwise you'll risk to end up with the mutiny) and so on. Sounds kinda cool (I mean, who doesn't like some extra micromanagement?), but it all ends up being a pretty annoying chore. Seriously, all that is so annoying that it may ruin your experience with the exploration. When you'll realize just how much time you'll need to waste on your crew just to travel to a distant island, you may actually decide that it isn't worth it and just stick with the main story instead.

Which... is not that good here either. To say the least. Follow the god (this series and its bloody gods...), talk with him a couple of times, enjoy the ending. Well, I'm I'm exaggerating, of course, because you'll need to make some big choices and those will have an impact on how things will end for the entire world at the end of the game, but since it's pretty hard to start caring about all of those gods, tribes and other stuff... let's just say it's not the most exciting journey you can ever imagine. Heck, I actually enjoyed some of the optional quests here more than I enjoyed the main story. Especially when we're talking about the companions.

Talking 'bout companions, by the way. Finally, we've got ourselves the romances. Which is good enough already, but guess what? Gender in [b]Pillars of Eternity 2[/b] is not a problem at all, so... it's all about the character you like. You have a character you like? As long as the character comes with the romance option, you can romance him or her. I kinda... fail to understand why in the bloody world [b]Obsidian[/b] didn't let us romance the cutest companions out there (like [b]Mirke[/b] or [b]Fassina[/b]), but still, I totally loved their approach on romances here. Moreover, the entire reputation system was re-worked [i]and[/i] your companions can even have affairs of their own now. [i]How cool is that?![/i]

So, it's not like [b]Pillars of Eternity 2[/b] is a bad game. Quite the opposite. There's a lot of good here. Like... [i]a lot[/i] of it. It's just when it's about old-school [b]RPG[/b]s, I would rather get something smaller, but with more attention to details. [b]Obsidian[/b] came up with some really interesting ideas, they've created a pretty big world, but failed to fill it with enough content and as the result, the game got a very unpleasant aftertaste. Up to the point where it may actually be more fun with cheats that allow you to ignore managing the crew completely. So... yeah. A lot of potential here. But potential alone doesn't exactly mean a good game. I still do recommend this game for all of us old-school [b]RPG[/b] fans out there, of course, just keep in mind that there's a lot of questionable things here. Like... A LOT of them.

I enjoyed this. Tho it does sort of overstay its welcome, at least with added DLC. 
You reach the level cap of 20 long before you are done with the content, so for me it did not feel very satisfying to continue doing sidequests and such. 
So after a certain point I just ignored them all and rushed the main story to finish the game.

The Good: the game is quite fun. The tactical combat can be quite challenging, and interesting. There are lots of places to see, characters to talk to, and moral dilemmas to consider. The epilogue felt like a satisfying accumulation of my decisions along the way. The story definitely fits well with the Pillars mythology and is a good sequel to the original game. I got 80 hours of fun game play out of the game, and hadn't quite tapped all the game's potential. Worth the money. I'd buy a sequel.

The Bad: director Josh Sawyer said that sales of this game were low and he didn't know why. I can explain what the missing "je ne sais quoi" is from my perspective. While the game is fun (as stated above), the story is very fragmented. There are tons of side quests and factions to support, but the main storyline is pretty short and not well-developed at all. The game starts off well, with lots of richness in the story and characters, but that fragments into a ton of little side quests and things to keep you occupied. Don't get me wrong, those things are fun, but they don't add up to a story that feels really satisfying. There are plenty of hack & slash and MMO games that offer tons of diverting side quests. I think people play an Obsidian game for the story. Pillars of Eternity II did not deliver here. The ending is interesting, but getting there felt... meh.

The Ugly: (1) two of the playable characters are cardboard cutouts--this is apparently due to the game having gotten insufficient funding from backers. Some of the characters are full of personality and have things to say at various points in the game, and have their own personal quest and epilogue, whereas there are a few that say virtually nothing and seem like ghosts. I would have preferred that the cardboard cutouts be removed entirely rather than haunting the game. (2) I didn't really like *any* of the factions presented. They were all unlikeable in my opinion. At least, on the bright side, the game-makers gave me the option to go independently.

It took 5 tries for me to enjoy this game. It starts slow, is plagued by performance issues, and requires the right mental space to enjoy. If you are patient and in the mood for reading lots of lore and dialogue, if you want to really get into your character in a pirate-y/ political intrigue/rogueish world this can be really enjoyable. Get it on a sale, relax and take a week off work, then immerse yourself in the world/ characters for a really enjoyable, memorable game.

I love these types of narrative-driven isometric rpg's, and obsidian is a benchmark in that regard, but when it comes to PoE 2, the technical side of things completely ruins the immersion and general experience for me. 

To be more precise - it's the loading times. Individual loading screens don't take that long, especially on SSD, it can range between ~10-40 seconds (longer on HDD), BUT the way the gameplay is designed, you are forced to travel between small zones ALL THE TIME, and these short loading screens really start to pile up. 
The gameplay in big cities (which you spend a looot of time at) is as follows: Loading screen > small area > dialogue > loading screen > small area > dialogue > loading screen... you get the point, 
The game discourages you from exploring, because you know you'll have to look at the black screen again and again and again. 
And as the game progresses it gets worse, data piles up, you have more items, more stuff to load - loading screens are longer and you have even more small rooms to visit.
I tried this game on 3 different PC's: my old Athlon x4 4gb ram, geforce 650ti, HDD: my work PC with core i7 7700, 128GB RAM (yes) and geforce 1060, SSD; and my new upgraded PC Ryzen 1600x, 16GB RAM, 1070TI 
Performance varied, but it sucked in all cases.

To conclude: i recommend against playing this game, unless you are 100% sure you can handle the frustration, it's not  a bad game but a good game that won't let you enjoy it.

The next game in the Pillars of Eternity series is an interesting specimen. Overall it is a great improvement over the first game. There’s full voice acting, graphics are improved (marginally from what I can tell),  combat is “improved” (We will get to that), and they added sailing and ship battles, cool! However there are some issues that I have with this game that need to be discussed. In this review I will break down the game and discuss various categories including: Factions, plot, combat, ships and sailing mechanics.

Factions:
The faction system has been greatly expanded over the first game. You now have primary factions that branch off into several different secondary factions that are roughly related to the primary factions in some way. Four of these primary factions can be joined and have their own quests to complete. You have the Principi, the pirate faction (you can guess what they are about). The Vallian Trading Company, they are about making as much money as possible through mostly legal means. The Royal Deadfire Company, they try to maintain order and law around the Deadfire. And finally the Huana, who are the natural inhabitants of the Deadfire and try to keep their culture alive and in power. Each of the factions is shown as being “morally gray” with no clear good or evil option. They all have their own agendas and sometimes use shady tactics to get what they want. The player technically doesn’t have to side with any of the factions if they don’t want to. The ending when you have to reach Ukaizo will be a bit more difficult but the game lets you not pick sides if you don’t want to. Based on your actions you can lose or gain reputation with a faction. Having high or low reputation does have an effect on gameplay whether it's through dialogue or affecting whether certain guards are hostile or not. In the end I think the faction system is well done. Each one is unique and has its advantages and disadvantages. This was one of the exceptionally designed aspects of the game in my opinion.

Plot:
The main plot is pretty simple but it works. Eothas ( the god of light, renewal, redemption, rebirth), has somehow materialized himself into the giant adra statue underneath Caed Nua and digs himself out. This destroys your fortress from the first game and ends up killing you. Eothas then starts treading far across the land destroying and killing everyone and everything in his path as he makes his way to Ukaizo so he can break the wheel, stopping the process of reincarnation and trapping all the souls in the in-between. Your character is then brought back to life by the god Berath with the catch of being her servant and tasked with stopping Eothas.
So, throughout the main story you are following Eothas’s footsteps to find where he is and try to talk him down of what he's doing. However, along the way as you progress your quest, you will be forced into councils with the various gods who debate and argue on what to do with Eothas and Kith, with the option to chime in once in a while to voice your opinion. You will eventually have to make a choice if you agree with what Eothas is trying to do or not, however I don’t think there is much of a difference. I might be wrong but I don’t think you can actually stop Eothas from breaking the wheel, but you can tell him how you feel and tell him how to “inspire” Kith to move on after the wheel is destroyed. I think the main plot and villain was more nuanced in the first game. Thaos, while he had his problems with how they incorporated him in the story, was still a much more interesting character and “villain” than Eothas in my opinion. I hesitate to even call Eothas a villain since while yes he is murdering a lot of people just to get to Ukaizo, couldn’t he have at least tried to be a bit more careful not to step on people along the way? But his end goal wasn’t really malicious and he is viewed as more of a “morally gray” character. Of which is a recurring theme with all the characters in this game, there really are no “villains” except maybe the Crookspur slavers or the vampire lord in Splintered Reef but they are such a small part of the game. Overall I think the plot is one of the weakest aspects of the game, being so simple and lacking much real choice in the end.

Combat:
The combat is mostly the same from the first game. One big change is that now each spell and ability are all per encounter instead of per rest. This lessens the amount of down time between encounters. Since spells and abilities are all per encounter, there is almost no need to rest. You can go through one tough encounter to the next without having to manage your spells or needing to stop and heal. Another big change was how the health system works. In the first game characters had health and endurance. When they took damage, their endurance would lower along with a small amount of health. When their endurance reaches zero, they would be knocked out and would re awaken after the battle is over or by being revived from a spell or scroll. After a battle endurance would regenerate, but health did not. To regain health, you had to rest. Now in Pillars 2, you no longer have endurance, instead it’s just health and “injuries”. Your health works the same way endurance works in Pillars 1. Injuries would occur if a character takes damage in some special way like through failing a skill check, or sometimes, but rarely, in combat. Once a character becomes injured 3 times, they die. I actually don’t really know what happens at that point because that never happened to me, but I am assuming they have to be revived in some special way. To recover from injuries, you have to rest. There are also special bonuses that can be gained from resting, like in Pillars 1. These are gained by resting at an inn, or by resting with certain types of food that you have on you when out in the field. So, you no longer need to rest to regain your spells, abilities, or heal. Now the only reasons to rest are to recover from injuries or to gain some bonuses to your stats. Honestly it’s hard to say which system is better for combat and resting mechanics. The original focused on resource management and made each fight feel like there is more on the line. You can’t just throw all of your spells and abilities at the enemies constantly and have to decide which is necessary to use depending on the situation. While in Pillars 2, being able to use your full arsenal in every fight does allow you to utilize and experiment more spells and abilities than you otherwise would if you were limited. This does also have the consequence of making each spell and ability feel less special and makes each fight feel more homogeneous. Ultimately I think I prefer the system in Pillars 1 which takes its inspiration from D&D and the infinity engine games.
	One last important thing to note about the combat is that there is an option now to pick either real time with pause or turn-based. I actually picked turned-based for my playthrough.  Even though the first game was RTWP, I wanted to try something new this time around. Well lets just say I ended up regretting that choice about half way through the game. The game was originally designed as RTWP, like Pillars 1. However turn-based was added later as an update, and it shows. The turn-based mode functions fine and actually feels pretty good for the most part. The problem however is that many encounters were not designed with turn-based in mind and also the dexterity stat becomes pretty much useless. Some combat encounters start really far away from enemies, so you have to sit through turn after turn to slowly get your characters over to the enemies in order to actually attack them or do something. Luckily this is pretty rare and I can only think of a couple instances when this happened, but it was rather annoying and concerning.

Let me start by saying that I really love this game - I think it is great - but, it has these really pressing, head-scratching flaws that make it frustrating for me to recommend out the gate. I played Deadfire with several mods aimed at trying to get to the core of the experience - I'd already played through the first act of the game on turn based mode several years ago, so I was familiar with the base systems and knew what I wanted. There are a few Community Patch mods that are used for serious bugfixing and power balancing on the game which I installed, plus a few others - the ability to fully respec/customize my companions' classes and stats (ala BG3), a mod that slowed down my experience gain substantially to stop me from hitting max level halfway through the campaign, and Unity Console which enabled me to debug and manually override some issues that arose from previous mods (as well as at least two gamebreaking bugs I ran into that aren't fixed by the Community Patches). All in all this was in service of me wanting to deeply engage with the game as much as possible, not sand away its edges. I played in real-time-with-pause mode now, which is substantially better than Turn Based, and on PotD difficulty.

I'll start with the good - I really love the Pillars RPG system and feel like Deadfire expanded and improved upon it in such a meaningful, valuable way. The classes all feel incredibly differentiated with their primary and subclass options, multiclassing offers so much exciting build variety, and the progression of powers + talents throughout the experience just makes for an incredibly deeply satisfying journey through building up your character.

Deadfire also corrects on a ton of Pillars 1's problems - they improved up on the original's mechanics really meaningfully, and I already enjoyed the original! The base systems, items, mechanics of this game are just really fucking good.

Narratively, I find the setup of Deadfire to be actually really great, and I love the entire story of the game. The factions are nuanced and interesting, without any clear true "bad guys" - don't get me wrong, Rauataians are ruthless colonialists, but when you talk to them, they have clear, pressing reasons for why they feel a burden of responsibility for securing the archipelago for their people (I was pretty staunchly anti-Rauatai regardless, but the narrative not painting any one faction out to be mustache-twirling villains is really refreshing. People are people at the end of the day.) Eothas is a fantastic antagonist, the expansion of worldbuilding between Pillars 1 and Deadfire is super exciting, I love interacting with the Gods more and more existential questions of the world - in my opinion it's all pretty good stuff. But -

It's not all good though. To start, the game has some meaningful bug and balance issues without the Community patches, which is honestly a bit surprising to me given how long it's been out. They're not subtle things either, like some abilities just straight up don't scale when they're supposed to, or scale off the wrong weapon. It's... weird to me that Obsidian hasn't gone in and fixed these things after so many years.

Narratively, while I find the worldbuilding and the conceit setup of the game to be super compelling and well done - like, greatly well done - I find the writing of individual characters to have taken a big step back between Pillars 1 and Deadfire. To the point where I wonder if they split up the narrative oversight of these departments? Pillars 1 had a score of interesting characters - there were some misses, at least for me, but I found most of them to be super interesting and well written characters in their own ways. By comparison, Deadfire's character writing feels distractingly uninspired and bland. Reading feedback online, I see a lot of people complaining that Pillars 1 was too wordy, too confusing, too serious, and that they wanted more light hearted romps from Deadfire and - god, I couldn't agree less. Pillars 1 was this flash of light of a genuinely compelling, meaningful, heartfelt narrative in a fantasy world that felt real because the people and the world felt real and that means that things are messy and uncomfortable and complicated and I loved that. Deadfire seems to have taken that feedback in stride and it is worse for it. Their characters feel more like caricatures of people, existing as billboards for their represented faction and objects for the Watcher to romance (another feature that was added in Deadfire that didn't exist in Pillars 1). Even returning characters are victim to this.

Mechanically, companions also have some frustrating stuff going on. Deadfire by default hard locks their stats - cannot modify - and gives you three options for classes - a solo class or two multiclass options. I can understand this on paper but I find it to be incredibly short-sighted, because it locks SO MUCH OF THE GAMEPLAY to only the Watcher. Deadfire has 60 subclasses total that the Watcher MC has access to - before multiclassing. But then your Companions are incredibly gated - very few of them even have multiclasses, and those that do are often weird and clunky. Serafen's Wild Mind Cipher is extremely swingy RNG that can win or lose you fights. Pallegina's Paladin subclass is just straight-up really bad and reworks a base ability to make it a good bit worse, while also being bugged and not scaling her defenses with her beliefs like other Paladins do. Tekehu's Druid subclass is very strong - but he has 10 base Perception, making his accuracy with the storm attacks he gains frustratingly low. 

Deadfire gets in its own way here - you want to bring Companions along for their narrative potential and integration. But, if you want to engage in the glory that is Deadfire's class design, you need to make custom Hirelings that have no narrative interaction whatsoever. And even if you do bring Companions with their own subclasses - many of their stat layouts don't make sense for the subclasses. This is why I downloaded the respec mods - so I could customize the stats and class/subclass of all of my companions, functionally giving me Hireling gameplay but with Companion narrative. I don't understand why they'd invest so much in having 60 subclasses but only give you access to them on one character unless you hire NPCs or do multiple playthroughs.

Progression, while mechanically satisfying, is also super poorly paced in Deadfire. I installed a mod to help with this, slowing down my exp gain, but I still hit max level well before I was done with any of the three DLCs, let alone the entire campaign story. This is... weird, to say the least. I did basically 100% the game - aside from one bounty that was bugged so I couldn't complete it - so I'm not surprised I was overleveled. But I was probably sitting at max level for about 15, maybe 20% of my Deadfire playtime which just feels very wrong to me. 

And finally, on the bugs, I ran into a few I could not fix without Unity Console interventions. I ran into technical problems throughout Deadfire that are disappointingly serious and I'm thankful I installed mods to be able to force-redirect around them.

However, in spite of all of this - the flattened, goofy character writing, the progression pacing issues, the bugs, the friction between gameplay and narrative when considering companions - I love Deadfire's combat, itemization, classes, and worldbuilding so much that this is still EASILY one of my favorite games I played in 2025. 

I love this game. I desperately hope they make a Pillars 3 and improve on the foundation they had here. If you do play it, I highly recommend at least the Community Patch + Extra mods, if not a few others for progression and respecc'ing.
