TL;DR:
If you  like games like Divinity: Original Sin, Baldur's Gate, Tyranny, etc. then you will probably like this game. You don't have to have played Pillars of Eternity 1 to understand what's going on in this one, but it would help.

Long version:
PoE2 is a story-heavy game that requires you to read a lot of text to keep up with what's happening, but not as much as PoE1. A lot (relatively) of the game includes voice acting, which helps it feel less like a visual novel, and the voice acting is superb in my opinion. I'm not very good at planning out talking points, so here are some random points that I think are important when considering whether or not you want to play this game:

PRIOR KNOWLEDGE REQUIRED?
You can totally play this as a standalone game without having played PoE1; there are some things in this game that might throw you off without the knowledge from the first game and definitely some things you will appreciate more having played the first game, but it's fairly easy to understand what's going on without that knowledge. They also do this cool thing where pretty much all of the keywords that reference something in-universe are highlighted, allowing you to hover over them with your cursor and read a short blurb defining that word and providing necessary context. I thought that was a great alternative to having to constantly check a humongous codex or whatever, which really breaks my immersion. 

RTWP OR TURN-BASED?
They chose to offer both. You have to pick which one you want at the beginning of the game and it cannot be swapped back and forth once you decide, but it's cool to have the option. Having played the game using both options, I personally prefer real time with pause as I've done all the fights before and am more interested in the story than the combat. Using turn-based combat makes the combat take a LOT longer, which has its pros and cons. On one hand, you get to appreciate the unique animations for spells and attacks, you get to plan out your combat encounters way more efficiently, and you're able to notice and counter certain afflictions and statuses WAY more effectively when it's not all happening at once, among other things. On the other, again, combat can drag on for what feels like ages, especially when the computer is taking its turns. Not that the enemies are particularly slow to react or anything (generally), but if you get in a fight with a lot of enemies it can feel like you're just watching combat happen for a bit. I also found that combat encounters were somewhat easier to win on turn-based mode, but maybe that's not the case for everyone.
 
OPEN WORLD?
Once you finish the first few required quests to get the story going, you're released into the open world and while you obviously CAN travel wherever you want, you will be... encouraged (maybe forced) to continue on a somewhat linear path which could feel like railroading to some people. The difficulty level is not balanced to be at your level, so if you wander too far from intended locations of the quest you're currently on, you can quite easily run into some enemies that you are not actually capable of beating, which is why it can feel linear. Once you reach a certain level, however, (about halfway through the game at least) you'll be strong enough to take on most enemies and will find very few obstacles that can truly prevent you from progressing. Regardless, I highly endorse saving the game OFTEN so you can just jump back to a save before the obstacle and take a different path, otherwise you could end up being very angry if your last save was hours ago and you're now stuck.

COMPANIONS/ROMANCE?
I think Obsidian generally does a great job making interesting companion characters, and this game is no exception. If you have played Obsidian games in the past and you didn't like the characters, you'll disagree. Obviously you have some characters from the first game, but the majority of the cast is new characters. As with most games like this, you'll likely find your favorite combination of characters to fill out your party and stick with them the whole game, never learning much about the other characters, which I think is fine. If you like to spend a lot of time talking to your companions and learning stuff about them like I do, they all have pretty interesting and dramatic backstories that they will continue to reveal to you the higher your approval rating is with them. It's possible that you may not actually find all of the available companions that can be recruited in the game (where my Rekke fans at?!) which can also add some value to replaying the game if desired. The "romance" in this game is pretty lackluster, consisting exclusively of a few dialogue options, maybe one off-hand comment about your preference for a specific character by your companions ("you and blank seem to spend a lot of time together!" etc.), more approving/romantic(?) barks when you select or control your romanced companion, and a slide or two about your future together (or not) in the end-game slideshow. There is almost zero recognition of your romantic partner by anyone in the game besides them, and you miss out on very little by entirely ignoring the romance aspect of the game. It definitely feels like an afterthought that was added last minute, especially considering the first game didn't have it at all.

CLASSES?
There are a variety of classes, generally the ones you'd probably expect from most D&D-inspired RPGs or other Obsidian games, as well as multi-classing to have even more control over customizing your character's abilities. You can also multi-class your companions, though you choose it when they join your team and it cannot be changed later. When you recruit a companion, you are presented with 3 options: Class 1, Class 2, and Multi-class 1 + 2. (e.g. Fighter, Rogue, Swashbuckler (fighter + rogue)) Leveling up is generally pretty easy to understand and streamlined, I'm someone who gets very easily confused and overwhelmed by complex skill trees and whatnot and I didn't have any issues. Some players might see that as a lack of customization, but i believe there's enough to constitute several specific builds or specializations per class.

DO CHOICES MATTER?
Throughout the game you will be asked to choose between one of two factions several times until you have amassed your end-game posse. Ultimately the story beats are mostly unchanged no matter what you choose, but who shows up to help at the end of the game will be the factions with whom your approval rating is the highest. It's not nearly as black-and-white as that makes it sound, but that's the gist of it. It's based on a relatively complex reputation system that affects how NPCs treat you; you will have a general reputation that is considered the opinion of the world at large and then you have a reputation with each of your companions. It's all based on the choices you make and your actions, and it will decide how you approach the end-game and can result in whole factions disowning you and your companions abandoning you. So yes, your choices matter.

SO SHOULD I PLAY IT?
I personally thoroughly enjoy this game, it's probably one of my favorites. If you liked games that are similar to it, you'll probably like it (obvious point is obvious). It doesn't stray far from the expected trajectory of an RPG made in 2018 and will likely not surprise you if you've played similar games. But, you get to explore a big map with lots of fun, hidden secrets in your very own boat that you can customize and give a hilarious name, who wouldn't want that?

Pillars of Eternity II: Deadfire is a rich, sprawling role-playing game that masterfully builds on the foundation of its predecessor while carving out a distinct identity through its bold setting, refined mechanics, and ambitious storytelling. Developed by Obsidian Entertainment, the game continues the narrative from the first Pillars of Eternity, placing the player in the role of the Watcher—a character capable of seeing into souls—now tasked with pursuing a resurrected god across the high seas of the Deadfire Archipelago. This sequel takes the familiar isometric RPG formula and injects it with a vibrant sense of exploration, offering players an expansive world filled with meaningful choices, political intrigue, and nuanced character development.

One of Deadfire’s greatest strengths lies in its dynamic world-building. The archipelago setting is a brilliant departure from the typical grim medieval environments of classic CRPGs, embracing a lush, tropical aesthetic full of color, life, and cultural diversity. The game’s world feels alive, with factions vying for control, towns bustling with activity, and islands shrouded in mystery waiting to be uncovered. Players are given command of their own ship, which serves not only as a hub of operations but as a mobile base that can be customized and upgraded. Naval travel and ship combat add a unique layer to exploration, and discovering new islands or navigating political waters becomes as engaging as the combat and quests.

The narrative structure of Deadfire is flexible and expansive, allowing players to pursue the main story at their own pace while getting lost in dozens of intricately written side quests and faction storylines. The main plot—centered around the god Eothas and questions of divinity, mortality, and power—serves as an epic backdrop for the game’s more intimate tales. What sets Deadfire apart is its commitment to player agency. Decisions made early on can ripple through the world in unexpected ways, altering relationships, shaping alliances, and even determining the fate of entire regions. The game consistently offers morally complex choices, rarely presenting obvious “good” or “evil” outcomes, which lends a sense of weight to every major decision.

Combat in Deadfire is deep and versatile, allowing players to switch between real-time with pause and full turn-based modes, depending on preference. The real-time mode is reminiscent of the original Infinity Engine games, requiring tactical positioning, cooldown management, and effective use of character abilities. The turn-based option, added in a later update, slows the pace but increases clarity, making it ideal for players who want more control over every move. The class system is robust, with dozens of unique classes and subclasses to choose from, including multiclassing, which allows for highly customized builds. Every party member can be tailored to complement others, and synergies between skills can be incredibly satisfying to discover and master.

Companions in Deadfire are another highlight, each with their own backstories, motivations, and character arcs that unfold naturally over the course of the game. Interactions with these companions—whether through personal quests, in-party banter, or moral disagreements—add a strong emotional layer to the journey. Characters like Eder, Pallegina, and the mysterious Serafen feel like real individuals, and the relationships players develop with them can influence key story moments. The game’s writing is consistently sharp, blending philosophical musings with wit and charm, and dialogue options often reflect the player’s background, class, race, and previous choices.

Graphically, Pillars of Eternity II is a step above its predecessor, with beautifully rendered environments, dynamic weather effects, and fluid animations. The hand-painted aesthetic brings each island and city to life, while the UI is clean and informative, making inventory and party management easy to navigate. The voice acting is strong across the board, enhancing immersion and bringing each character to life with distinct personalities. The game’s soundtrack, composed by Justin E. Bell, is a standout as well, capturing the spirit of adventure and mystery that permeates the world of Deadfire.

In conclusion, Pillars of Eternity II: Deadfire is an outstanding sequel that evolves the CRPG genre by taking bold creative risks and executing them with skill and care. Its expansive world, thoughtful storytelling, deep customization, and meaningful player choice make it one of the finest examples of modern role-playing design. While it caters most directly to fans of classic RPGs, its engaging characters and accessible systems offer something for any player seeking a rich and immersive narrative experience. Deadfire is not just a continuation of a great story—it’s a voyage into a world that feels genuinely alive, and one well worth setting sail for.

So the last 2 years I've been playing some isometric RPGs. First Pillars of Eternity then Tyranny, Shadowrun series and Baldur's Gate series. Now Pillars 2 is finally out I couldn't wait to get my hands on it. Much more detailed character models, beautiful environments, brilliant soundtrack, full voice over, and the most important multipath storytelling. All these improvements quickly suck me right into Eora again.

What I really enjoy playing RPGs are mostly for multipath storytelling. Here's an example. After I gained control to my ship, a "friend" approached me with his ship hunting buddy, asked me to get rid of his pain-in-the-butt rival, lent me his ship hunting buddy and set me onto my target's fortress. The ship hunting buddy told me I had 3 ways to get to my target: frontal assault which is high unadvisable, sneak in under nightfall but my companion are not all suitable for this task, or disguise my ship with a faction flag. I happened to plunder a ship that grant me a proper flag to get me into the fortress without causing a fuss. In the fortress I dabbled here and there, got drunk with a bunch of pirates, sneak into the dungeons, rescued some quatermaster's buddies and he grant me access to the fortress' western rampart so I could fire up a mutiny for him. But I prefer more subtle appraoch. I sneak to the eastern rampart, stole my target's finest brew, got to start a assassination party, sabotaged his piano. When he got to perform for fun, that's the last thing he ever did in his life. That kind of Hitman style is exactly how I want to play as my character.

Commanding my own ship, charting through out Deadfire Archipelago takes me back to the time when I really enjoyed flying Normandy around the galaxy map in Mass Effect. But this time I have to be careful managing my crew and ration to keep up high moral, until I have enough money to stock up 1000 units of fruit and water (and it's hilarious to imagine everybody on my ship becomes vegetarian XD), I can unravel every corner of the map with ease. Ship combat at first gave me an illusion that I need to lay out my tactics carefully in order to survive, then it quickly became ramming into every enemy and starting mayhem. The money I gathered by pirating goes towards purchasing better weapons and armor, never bother with the ship upgrades. With developing resources limited I can overlook the drawback that every ship combat is text-walled. It's not boring at least, I had fun overcome the odds to plunder higher level ships and triumph.

Main story has its potential but feels a bit lacking. The immediate threat of Eothas is quickly pushed aside by side quests that are more interesting both in story and perspective. I can see Pillars II looks up to its predecessor Baldur's Gate II, as a matter of fact a lot of cRPGs after that time followed the similar path. Sometimes it works, other times it doesn't. In this case, Eothas' "you-kith-can-not-comprehend-my-purpose" delay at first half of the story doesn't quite make sense because we mortals' IQ are not as low as my room's temperature. The effort goes towards world building is phenomenal, and I appreciate it.

Companion relationship seems fixed at first glance. But as I travel with them, I keep discovering hidden layers of relationship beneath it. It's really intriguing I might say. Companion quests are simple, with a conversation in the end that will decide their fate, except for Pellagina and Eder.

Character disposition seems bugged at the moment, NPCs tend to mention my less developed traits all the time. I play as a smartass Watcher, but often people recognize me as an aggro brute.

Combat feels great, it's everything I could've hoped for.

Overall it's a great ride, a lot of details tailored with love and passion won't go unnoticed. And here's the pros and cons that I feel like worth mentioning:

Pros:
+  Visual and model improvements
+ Soundtrack
+ Full voice acting
+ Writing
+ Some level designs are of the immersive sims style, I like it.
+ Attention to detail

Cons:
- Story pacing
- Nemnok, really, he should shut up most of the time, I can't hear party banter for Berath's sake.
- bugs, I haven't encountered a game breaking one, some are annoying nontheless.

Thank you, Obsidian, for a great game that I really enjoy. And here's a sincere suggestion that better developing resource management is in order if there's a better sequel to come. A compelling main story is a rare gem among RPGs these days, I hope you guys hold on to it.

Deadfire doesn't get the hype it deserves. The universe, characters, and voice acting are all top notch and immerse the player from the outset. RPG elements are quick to learn well enough to play, but deep to satisfy a fair amount of theory crafting. The tool tips leave something to be desired, but it is better in this regard than titles like pathfinder and worse than divinity. 
What this title does better than any of it's competitors is sell you on the world and characters through excellent radiant dialogue options with impactful player choices. Even small and irrelevant characters will have voice acting that is well above average in this genre and the quality of the voice acting for major characters and deities had me sold on the world and the title within the first hour of play. Almost everyone you meet has a bit of depth to them, and that's what makes an RPG world immerse you. 
The game does have it's struggles. Pacing is almost absent, as the player may find themselves overloaded with tasks and not sure what narrative direction the game is headed in at a particular time. Side quests bloat your quest log and the quest format takes the form of one chore leading to 3 more quickly. 
In conclusion if you enjoyed Divinity then Deadfire could be a great way to wade into another title of the genre that has more depth and is geared towards a solo experience.

Its got Obsidian's amazing writing/story telling, Its got Obsidian's amazing RP-ing, Its got more lore than a lore addict knows what to do with. Its great. 



All in all, if you like RPGs, fantastic characters and story telling, rich vibrant worlds, then this is a no brainer. Worth full price for sure.

Fantastic game, very fun!
Pros
- Excellent customisation and class choices.
- Kinetic combat, definitely not tedious, I actually found myself foregoing the turn based mode in favour of the real time, I almost always use turn based in games.
- Interesting environments and a story that you don't lose track of.
- The story book style choices and RPG choices is really fun and makes it feel like a choose your own adventure book. 
- The naval combat system and outfitting your ship is really fun, even if you aren't typically into that sort of thing.

Cons
- As much as I love the cast of critical role, you will get sick of hearing their voices over and over because they pretty much voice 80% of all NPCs in this game, this goes for major and minor characters.
- Though I don't think this is strictly applicable to Deadfire and more to the genre of game itself, but there are sudden and unforeseen difficulty jumps that will rim you. 
- There isn't a post game, instead it is point of no return which always sucks. 
- Sometimes it feels like there is too much to do, the content sometimes doesn't feel like a linear path which can lead to floundering. 
- Whilst this wasn't a con for me personally, I know it might be a selling point for some people. This is not a romance simulator! You can form different levels of attachment to characters but almost all of the pathways are very superficial and don't lead to any impact in the story. An event that happened to me at one stage was I did something that went against the morals of one of my teammate and they hated me even though I had done nothing but appease them throughout the entirety of the game.  Effectively, this game doesn't thrive with its character interactions at all, its strength comes from a variety of ways to complete objectives and missions.

Summary
Fast paced and fantastic game, solid customisation and a really awesome RPG experience. 
Character interactions and development is almost non existent, you will experience difficulty spikes that could halt your story progress indefinitely and there is repetition with the voice cast.

90% of this game is practically perfect. Combat is smooth. Understanding the leveling, gearing nuts and bolts was easy to grasp. The inclusion of the turn based combat system was seamless. 

It's the 10% that isn't perfect that will make or break this game for some people. The overall 'problem' that made the game a bit of a slog to get into/through was the writing as a whole.

The main thrust of the story (Chasing after a God who stole your soul!) often suffers from pacing issues as your character repeatedly finds themselves bogged down by the decidedly lower stake problems of those around you. You will potentially spend hours or multiple gaming sessions messing around before stumbling back onto the path of reclaiming your soul. It's not ALL bad, mind you -- there are plenty of pirate fights, double crosses, and exploring old temples and tombs. Though from a narrative perspective, much (not all, but much) of the side questing felt tangential and served no purpose other than providing experience points and, much more rarely, useful loot/equipment. While not EVERY quest needs to be intrinsically tied with your search for your soul, the ones that don't also don't tend to provide much sense that what you are doing actually matters to anyone either, or otherwise improves/worsens the state of affairs in the setting. You're just sort of...handling inconveniences as opposed to performing heroic/villainous deeds. 

To complicate matters, you are often bombarded with novel pages of description of events and settings that does its best to remind you of playing tabletop games with your friends, but in the context of a video game, that lengthy description grinds the pace to a halt. Sometimes these descriptions are voice acted, but just as often they are not. Side quest givers can ramble for 5 or more lengthy dialogue entries for something as simple as a fetch quest or a find this person quest. Play through any level of Super Mario Bros., then stop and read 3 pages of any fantasy novel you have lying around before starting to play again; you'll have an idea of how "start and stop" the pacing of Deadfire can be. The writing staff needed to do a better job of getting across the important details without bogging the player and pacing down with mountains of purple prose and extraneous exposition.

Just can't get into it. Certainly an improvement over Pillars 1, but it still has many of the same issues, and ultimately just isn't that fun. Every combat ends up feeling the same once you have your party you execute the same strategy every time. While the classes feel decently balanced many of them are boring and a downright chore to play. And the stats, the worst stat system in any western RPG ever. Literally every character wants the same stats, you don't play a high int wizard, you play a high dex wizard, you don't play a high might fighter, you play a high dex fighter, dex is so obviously crushingly the best stat. At least in turn based you can use other stats but the fact that classes don't benefit from a primary stat, like this games obvious tabletop inspiration, is a glaring issue. The story is just another save the world chosen-one thing, maybe it changes later in the game, but I can't seem to find the will to even open the game.

Ultimately it's boring is the games biggest sin. I could probably forgive everything else, but even on the hardest difficulty combats are trivial unless you get incredibly unlucky. If you really absolutely love infinity engine style games you'll probably like this, but I just wouldn't recommend it.
